2.0.oldText: In a way, the child brought the parents back together. Over his little cradle they met in a common hope, a common joy, a common fear; they thought of him and they spoke of him, each as often and as readily as the other, and each was grateful to the other for the child and for all the happiness and love he brought.

2.1.oldText: Yet they were still far apart.

2.2.oldText: Lyhne was quite absorbed in his farming and the affairs of the parish. Not that he took the role of a leader or a reformer, but he gave scrupulous attention to the existing order of things, looked on as an interested spectator, and carried out the cautious improvements recommended, after deliberate — very deliberate — consideration, by his old head servant or by the elders of the parish.

2.3.oldText: It never occurred to him to make any use of the knowledge he had acquired in earlier days. He had too little faith in what he called theories and far too great a respect for the time-honored, venerable dogmas of experience that other people called practical. In fact, nothing about him indicated that he had not lived here and lived this way all his life — nothing except one small trait. He had a habit of sitting for half hours at a time, quite motionless, on a stile or a boundary stone, gazing out over the lush green rye or the golden, top-heavy oats in a strange, vegetative trance. That was the old Lyhne, the young Lyhne.

2.4.oldText: Bartholine, in her world, was nowhere near so ready to adapt herself quickly and with good grace. No, she first had to voice her sorrow through the verses of a hundred poets, lamenting, in all the broad generalities of the period, the thousands of barriers and fetters that oppress humanity. Sometimes her lament would be clothed in lofty indignation, flinging its wordy foam against the thrones of emperors and the dungeons of tyrants; sometimes it would take the form of a calm, pitying sorrow, watching the radiant light of beauty fade from a blind and slavish generation cowed and broken by the soulless bustle of the day; and then again it would appear only as a gentle sigh for the freedom of the bird in flight and of the cloud drifting lightly into the distance.

2.5.oldText: At last she grew tired of lamenting, and the impotence of her grief goaded her into doubt and bitterness. Like worshippers who beat their saint and trample him underfoot when he refuses to show his power, she would scoff at the romance she had once idolized, and ask herself scornfully whether she did not expect the bird Roc to appear presently in the cucumber bed, or Aladdin's cave to open under the floor of the milk cellar. She would answer herself in a kind of childish cynicism, pretending that the world was ridiculously prosaic, calling the moon green cheese and the roses potpourri — all with a sense of taking revenge and, at the same time, with a half uneasy, half fascinated feeling that she was committing blasphemy.

2.6.oldText: These attempts to set herself free came to nothing. She sank back into the dreams of her girlhood, but now with this difference: they were no longer lit by hope. And she had learned, too, that they were only dreams — distant, elusive dreams that no longing in the world could ever draw down to her earth. When she surrendered to them now, it was with a sense of weariness, while an accusing inner voice told her she was like the drunkard who knows his passion is destroying him, that every binge means strength taken from his weakness and added to the power of his desire. But the voice spoke in vain, for a sober life, lived without the fair vice of dreams, was no life at all — life had exactly the value that dreams gave it, and no more.

2.7.oldText: Such was the vast difference between Niels Lyhne's father and mother, the two friendly powers that struggled unconsciously for mastery over his young soul from the moment the first gleam of intelligence in him gave them something to work on. As the child grew older, the struggle grew more intense and was waged with a wider variety of weapons.

2.8.oldText: The faculty through which the mother tried to reach the boy was his imagination. He had plenty of imagination, but even when he was very small it was clear that he felt a great difference between the fairy world his mother's words conjured up and the world that really existed. His mother would often tell him stories and describe the woeful plight of the hero until Niels could see no way out of all this trouble and could not understand how the misery — closing tighter and tighter, like an impenetrable wall, around him and the hero — could possibly be overcome. Then more than once it happened that he would suddenly press his cheek against his mother's and whisper, with eyes full of tears and lips trembling, "But it isn't really true?" And when he had been given the comforting answer he wanted, he would heave a deep sigh of relief and settle down contentedly to hear the end.

2.9.oldText: His mother did not quite like this defection.

2.10.oldText: When he grew too old for fairy tales, and she grew tired of inventing them, she began to tell him — with some embroideries of her own — about the heroes of war and peace, choosing those who lent themselves to pointing a moral about the power that dwells in a human soul when it wills one thing only, and will neither let itself be discouraged by the short-sighted doubts of the moment nor be lured into a soft, enervating peace.

2.11.oldText: All her stories went to this tune, and when history ran out of heroes that suited her, she chose an imaginary hero — one whose deeds and fate she could shape as she pleased. A hero after her own heart: spirit of her spirit, yes, flesh of her flesh and blood of hers, too.

2.12.oldText: A few years after Niels was born, she had brought forth a stillborn boy, and him she chose. Everything he might have been and done she served up before his brother in a confused medley of Promethean longings, Messianic courage, and Herculean strength, with a naïve travesty, a monstrous distortion, a world of cheap fantasies that had no more body of reality than did the tiny little skeleton mouldering in the earth of Lönborg graveyard.

2.13.oldText: Niels was not deceived about the moral of all these tales. He understood perfectly that it was contemptible to be like ordinary people, and he was quite ready to submit to the hard fate that belonged to heroes. In his imagination he willingly endured the wearisome struggles, the ill fortune, the martyrdom of being misunderstood, and the victories without peace. Yet at the same time he felt a marvelous relief in thinking that it was all so far away, that none of this would happen before he was grown up.

2.14.oldText: As the dream-figures and dream-tones of night may walk abroad in the waking day like vapory forms, mere shadows of sound, calling on thought and holding it for a fleeting second as it listens and wonders whether anyone really called — so the images of that dream-born future whispered softly through Niels Lyhne's childhood, reminding him gently but ceaselessly that there was a limit to this happy time, and that one day, before long, it would be no more.

2.15.oldText: This awareness stirred in him a craving to enjoy his childhood to the full, to drink it up through every sense, not to spill a drop, not a single one. And so his play had an intensity — sometimes lashed into a passion — under the pressure of an uneasy feeling that time was flowing away from him before he could gather, from its treasure-laden waters, all they brought, as wave broke upon wave. He would sometimes throw himself down on the ground and sob in despair when a holiday hung heavy on his hands for lack of one thing or another — playmates, inventiveness, or fair weather — and he hated going to bed, because sleep was empty of events and devoid of sensation.

2.16.oldText: Yet it was not always like this.

2.17.oldText: It sometimes happened that he grew weary and his imagination ran out of colors. Then he would be quite wretched, feeling that he was too small and insignificant for these ambitious dreams. He seemed to himself a mean liar who had brazenly pretended to love and understand what was great, though in truth he cared only for the petty, loved only the commonplace, and carried within him, fully alive, all those low-born wishes and desires. Sometimes he would even feel that he had the class hatred of the rabble against everything exalted, and that he would joyfully have helped to stone those heroes who were of better blood than he and knew it.

2.18.oldText: On such days he would shun his mother and, with a sense of following an ignoble instinct, seek out his father, turning a willing ear and receptive mind to his earth-bound thoughts and matter-of-fact explanations. He felt at home with his father and rejoiced in the likeness between them, almost forgetting that this was the same father whom he was used to looking down upon with pity from the pinnacles of his dream-castle. Of course this was not present in his childish mind with the clarity and definiteness that the spoken word would have given it, but it was all there — though unformed, unborn, in a vague and intangible embryo form. It was like the strange vegetation at the bottom of the sea seen through layers of ice. Break the ice, or draw out into the full light of speech what lives in the dimness — and what happens is the same: the thing now seen and now grasped is not, in its clearness, the shadowy thing it was.

3.0.oldText: The years passed. One Christmas trod on the heels of another, leaving the air bright with its festive glow long after Epiphany. Whitsun after Whitsun scampered across flower-decked meadows. One summer holiday after another drew near, celebrated its orgy of fresh air and sunshine, poured out its fiery wine from brimming goblets, and then vanished, one day, into a sinking sun — only memory lingered, with sunburnt cheeks and wondering eyes and blood that danced.

3.1.oldText: The years had passed, and the world was no longer the realm of wonder it had been. The dim recesses behind the mouldering elder bushes, the mysterious attic rooms, the gloomy stone passage under the Klastrup road — the imagined terrors that had once thrilled him no longer lurked there. The hillside that bloomed at the first trill of the lark, hiding the grass beneath starry, purple-rimmed daisies and yellow buttercups; the fantastic wealth of animals and plants in the river; the wild precipices of the sand-pit with its black rocks and chips of silvery granite — all these were simply flowers, animals, and stones; the shining fairy gold had turned back into withered leaves.

3.2.oldText: One game after another grew old and silly, stupid and tiresome like the pictures in a primer — and yet they had once been new, inexhaustibly new. Here they used to roll a barrel hoop — Niels and the pastor's Frithjof — and the hoop was a ship, which was wrecked when it toppled over, but if you caught it before it fell, then it was casting anchor. The narrow passage between the outbuildings, where you could hardly squeeze through, was Bab-el-Mandeb or the Portal of Death. On the stable door "England" was written in chalk, and on the barn door "France." The garden gate was Rio de Janeiro, and the smithy was Brazil. Another game was to play Holger the Dane: you could play it among the tall burrs behind the barn, but if you went up into the miller's pasture there were two sink-holes known as the gorges, and there were the haunts of the real Prince Burmand and his wild Saracens, with reddish-grey turbans and yellow plumes in their helmets — burdocks and Aaron's rod, the tallest of them. That was the only real Mauretania. That rank, succulent growth, that teeming mass of exuberant plant life, woke their lust of destruction and intoxicated them with the voluptuous joy of demolishing. The wooden swords gleamed with the brightness of steel; the green sap stained the blade with red gore; the cut stalks squelching under their feet were Turks' bodies trampled beneath horses' hooves with a sound as of bones crunched in flesh.

3.3.oldText: Sometimes they played down by the fjord: mussel shells were launched as ships, and when the vessel got stuck in a clump of seaweed or ran aground on a sandbank, it was Columbus in the Sargasso Sea or the discovery of America. Harbors and mighty embankments were built; the Nile was dug out in the firm beach sand; and once they made Gurre Castle out of pebbles — a tiny dead fish in an oyster shell was the corpse of Tove, and they were King Valdemar sitting sorrowing at her side.

3.5.oldText: Niels was quite a lad now, twelve years old and nearing thirteen, and he no longer needed to hack down thistles and burdocks to feed his knightly fancies, any more than he had to launch his explorer's dreams in a mussel shell. A book and a corner of the sofa were enough for him now, and if the book refused to bear him to the shores of his longing, he would hunt up Frithjof and tell him the tale the book would not yield. Arm in arm, they would saunter down the road, one telling, both listening; but when they wanted to revel in it fully and give their imagination free play, they would hide in the fragrant dimness of the hayloft. After a while these stories, which always ended just as you had really entered into them, grew into a single long story that never ended at all, but lived and died with one generation after another — for when the hero had grown old, or you had been careless enough to let him die, you could always give him a son, who would inherit everything from his father, and whom, besides, you could endow with any other virtues you happened to value particularly at the moment.

3.6.oldText: Whatever stamped itself on Niels's mind — what he saw, what he understood and what he misunderstood, what he admired and what he knew he ought to admire — all of it was woven into the story. As running water is colored by every picture passing over it, sometimes holding the image with perfect clearness, sometimes distorting it or flinging it back in wavering, uncertain lines, then again drowning it entirely in the color and play of its own ripples, so the lad's story reflected feelings and thoughts, his own and other people's, mirrored human beings and events, life and books, as best it could. It was a play-life, running alongside the real one. It was a snug retreat where you could abandon yourself to dreams of the wildest adventures. It was a fairy garden that opened at your slightest nod and received you in all its glory, shutting out everyone else. Whispering palms closed overhead; flowers of sunshine and leaves like stars on vines of coral spread at your feet, and among them a thousand paths led to every age and every clime. If you followed one, it led you to one place; if you followed another, it led you to another — to Aladdin and Robinson Crusoe, to Vaulunder and Henrik Magnard, to Niels Klim and Mungo Park, to Peter Simple and Odysseus — and the moment you wished it, you were home again.

3.7.oldText: About a month after Niels's twelfth birthday, two new faces appeared at Lönborggaard.

3.8.oldText: One was the new tutor; the other was Edele Lyhne.

3.9.oldText: The tutor, Mr. Bigum, was a candidate for holy orders, standing at the threshold of his forties. He was rather small, but with the stocky strength of a work-horse — broad-chested, high-shouldered, and slightly stooping. He walked with a heavy, slow, deliberate tread, and moved his arms in a vague, expressionless way that seemed to require a great deal of room. His high, wide forehead was flat as a wall, with two perpendicular lines between the eyebrows; the nose was short and blunt, the mouth large with thick, fresh lips. His eyes were his best feature, light in color, mild, and clear. The movement of his eyeballs betrayed that he was slightly deaf. Nevertheless he loved music and played his violin with passionate devotion, for the notes, he said, were not heard with the ears alone but with the whole body — eyes, fingers, and feet; if the ear failed at times, the hand would find the right note without its help, by a strange, intuitive genius of its own. Besides, the audible tones were, after all, only false, while the man who possessed the divine gift of music carried within him an invisible instrument compared to which the most wonderful Cremona was like the stringed calabash of a savage. On this instrument the soul played; its strings gave forth ideal notes, and upon it the great tone-poets had composed their immortal works.

3.10.oldText: The outer music, borne on the air of reality and heard with the ears, was nothing but a wretched imitation, a stammering attempt to say the unutterable. It resembled the music of the soul as the statue modeled by hands, carved with a chisel, and measured with a rule resembled the marvellous marble dream of the sculptor that no eye had ever beheld and no lip ever praised.

3.11.oldText: Music, however, was by no means Mr. Bigum's chief interest. He was first of all a philosopher — but not one of the productive philosophers who find new laws and build new systems. He laughed at their systems, those snail-shells in which they dragged themselves across the illimitable field of thought, fondly imagining that the field was inside the snail-shell! And these laws — laws of thought, laws of nature! Why, the discovery of a law meant nothing more than the fixing of your own limitations: I can see this far and no farther — as if there were not another horizon beyond the first, and another and yet another, horizon beyond horizon, law beyond law, in an unending vista! No, he was not that kind of philosopher. He did not think he was vain or that he overvalued himself, but he could not close his eyes to the fact that his intellect had a wider span than that of other mortals. When he meditated on the works of the great thinkers, it seemed to him that he strode forward through a region peopled by slumbering thought-giants, who awoke, bathed in the light of his spirit, to a consciousness of their own strength. And so it always went: every thought, mood, or sentiment of another person that was granted the privilege of awakening within him rose up with his sign on its forehead — ennobled, purified, its wings strengthened, endowed with a power and a might its creator had never dreamed of.

3.12.oldText: How often had he gazed with an almost humble amazement at the marvelous wealth of his soul and the divine assurance of his spirit! For it would often happen that different days found him judging the world and the things of the world from entirely divergent points of view, seeing them through hypotheses that were as far apart as night and morning — yet these points of view and hypotheses, which he chose to make his own, never for one second made him theirs, any more than the god who has taken the semblance of a bull or a swan becomes a bull or a swan and ceases to be a god.

3.13.oldText: And no one suspected what dwelt within him — everyone passed him by unseeing. But he rejoiced in their blindness and felt his contempt for humanity growing. A day would come when the light in his eye would go out, and the magnificent structure of his mind would crumble to its foundations and become as though it had never been — but no work from his hand, not a line, would he leave behind to tell the tale of what had been lost in him. His genius would not be crowned with thorns by the world's misjudgment, nor would it wear the defiling purple cloak of the world's admiration. He exulted at the thought that generation after generation would be born and die, and that the greatest men of every age would spend years of their lives trying to reach what he could have given them if only he had chosen to open his hand.

3.14.oldText: The fact that he lived in such a humble fashion gave him a curious pleasure, simply because there was such a magnificent extravagance in using his mind to teach children, such a wild incongruity in paying for his time with mere daily bread, and such a colossal absurdity in letting him earn that bread on the recommendation of poor, ordinary mortals who had vouched for him that he knew enough to take on the miserable task of a tutor. And they had given him a non on his examination for a degree!

3.15.oldText: Oh, there was rapture in feeling the brutal stupidity of an existence that tossed him aside as poor chaff and prized as golden grain the empty husks — while he knew in his own mind that his lightest thought was worth a world!

3.16.oldText: Yet there were other times when the solitude of his greatness weighed on him and pressed him down.

3.17.oldText: Ah, how often, after he had communed with himself in sacred silence, hour upon hour, and then returned to consciousness of the audible, visible life around him, had he not felt himself a stranger to its paltriness and decay. At such times he was often like the monk who listened in the monastery woods to a single trill of the bird of paradise and, when he came back, found that a century had died. If the monk was lonely among the generation that lived in the groves he had known, how much lonelier was the man whose contemporaries had not yet been born.

3.18.oldText: In such desolate moments he would sometimes be seized by a cowardly longing to sink down to the level of the common herd, to share their low-born happiness, to become a native of their great earth and a citizen of their little heaven. But soon he would be himself again.

3.19.oldText: The other newcomer was Edele Lyhne, Lyhne's twenty-six-year-old sister. She had lived for many years in Copenhagen, first with her mother, who had moved to the city when she was widowed, and, after her mother's death, in the home of a wealthy uncle, Councillor of State Neergaard. The Neergaards entertained on a large scale and went out a great deal, so Edele had lived in a whirl of balls and festivities.

3.20.oldText: She was admired wherever she went, and envy — the faithful shadow of admiration — also followed her. She was talked about as much as a woman can be without having done anything scandalous, and whenever men discussed the three reigning beauties of the town, there were always many voices in favor of striking out one name and substituting Edele Lyhne's. But they could never agree on which of the other two should yield to her — as for the third, it was out of the question.

3.21.oldText: Yet very young men did not admire her. They were abashed in her presence, and felt twice as stupid as usual when she listened to them with that look of mild toleration — a maliciously emphasized toleration that crushed them with the sense that she had heard it all before and knew it by heart. They made efforts to shine in her eyes and their own by affecting blasé airs, by inventing wild paradoxes, or, when desperation reached its climax, by making bold declarations; but all these attempts, jostling and crowding upon one another in the abrupt transitions of youth, were met with the faint shadow of a smile, a deadly smile of boredom, that made the victim redden and feel he was the one-hundred-and-eleventh fly caught in the same merciless spider's web.

3.22.oldText: Moreover, her beauty had neither the softness nor the fire to ensnare young hearts. On older hearts and cooler heads, however, it exerted a peculiar fascination.

3.23.oldText: She was tall. Her thick, heavy hair was blonde with the faint reddish sheen of ripening wheat, but fairer and curling where it grew in two points low on the nape of her neck. Beneath the high, clean-cut forehead, her eyebrows were pale and indefinite. The light grey eyes were large and clear, neither accented by the brows nor borrowing fitful shadows from the thin, delicate lids. There was something indeterminate, something unfathomable in their expression. They always met you with a full and open gaze, without any of the changeful play of sidelong glances or sudden flashes — but almost unnaturally wakeful, invincible, inscrutable. The vivacity was all in the lower part of the face — the nostrils, the mouth, the chin. The eyes merely looked on. The mouth was particularly expressive. The lips met in a lovely bow with deep, gracious curves and flexible lines, but their beauty was marred a little by a hardness of the lower lip, which sometimes melted away in a smile and then stiffened again into something close to brutality.

3.24.oldText: The bold sweep of her back and the luxuriant fullness of her bosom, set against the classical severity of her shoulders and arms, gave her an audacity, an exotic fascination, which was heightened by the gleaming whiteness of her skin and the morbid redness of her lips. The effect was provocative and disquieting.

3.25.oldText: Her tall, slender figure had a subtle distinction, which she was clever enough to underscore, especially in her ball gowns, with a sure and conscious art. In fact, her artistic sense applied to her own person would sometimes speak so loudly from her costume that it barely escaped a hint of bad taste even when most exquisitely tasteful. To many this seemed an added charm.

3.26.oldText: Nothing could have been more punctiliously correct than her behavior. In what she said, and in what she permitted to be said, she kept within the strictest bounds of prudery. Her coquetry consisted in not being coquettish — in being incurably blind to her own power and never making the slightest distinction between her admirers. For that very reason, they all dreamed intoxicating dreams of the face that must be hidden behind the mask; they believed in a fire under the snow and scented depravity in her innocence. None of them would have been surprised to hear that she had a secret lover, but neither would any of them have ventured to guess his name.

3.27.oldText: This was the way people saw Edele Lyhne.

3.28.oldText: She had left the city for Lönborggaard because her health had suffered from the constant round of pleasures, the thousand and one nights of balls and masquerades. Toward the end of winter, the doctor had declared her lungs to be affected and had prescribed fresh air, quiet, and milk. All these she found in abundance in her new abode — but she also found an unceasing boredom, which made her long for Copenhagen before a week had passed. She filled letter after letter with entreaties to be allowed back from her exile, hinting that homesickness was doing her more harm than the country air was doing good. But the doctor had so alarmed her uncle and aunt that they felt it their duty to turn a deaf ear to her lamentations, no matter how pathetic.

3.29.oldText: It was not so much the social diversions she pined for; it was rather that she craved the sense of feeling her own life mingling with the sound-filled air of the great city — whereas in the country, the stillness in thoughts, in words, in eyes, in everything, made her feel as though she heard herself unceasingly and with inescapable distinctness, the way one hears a watch ticking through a sleepless night. And to know that over there they were living exactly as before — it was as though she lay dead in the quiet night and heard the strains of music from a ballroom stealing across the air over her grave.

3.30.oldText: There was no one she could talk to. Not one of them ever caught the precise shade of meaning that was the essence of what she said. Of course, they understood her after a fashion, insofar as she spoke Danish, but in a dull, general sort of way, just as they might have understood a foreign language they heard only once in a while. They never had the slightest idea of whom or what was meant by a particular intonation of a word, never dreamed that such a little phrase was a quotation, or that another, used in just such a way, was a new variation on a popular witticism. As for their own speech, it had a decent leanness through which one could positively feel the grammatical ribs, and the words were used with a literalness as though they had just come fresh from the columns of a dictionary. Even the way they said Copenhagen! Sometimes with a mysterious emphasis, as if it were a place where people ate little children; sometimes with a faraway expression, as though they spoke of a town in central Africa; sometimes in a festive voice tremulous with history, as they might have said Nineveh or Carthage. The pastor always said Axelstead with a reminiscent rapture, as if it were the name of one of his old sweethearts. Not one of them could say Copenhagen so that it meant the city stretching from Vesterport to the Custom House, on both sides of Östergade and Kongens Nytorv. And so it was with everything they said and everything they did.

3.31.oldText: There was not a thing at Lönborggaard that did not displease her: these mealtimes regulated by the sun, this smell of lavender in chests and cupboards, these Spartan chairs, all these provincial pieces of furniture that stood shrinking against the walls as though they were afraid of people! Even the very air was distasteful to her; she could never go for a walk without bringing home a robust perfume of meadow hay and wild flowers, as though she had been locked up in a hay market.

3.32.oldText: And then to be called aunt — Aunt Edele. How it grated on her ears! She got used to it in time, but in the beginning it made the relationship between her and Niels rather cool.

3.34.oldText: Then came a Sunday in early August, when Lyhne and his wife had gone out in the carriage to pay a visit, and Niels and Miss Edele were home alone. That morning Edele had asked Niels to pick some cornflowers for her, but he had forgotten. Suddenly, in the afternoon, as he was walking with Frithjof, he remembered, gathered a bouquet, and ran up to the house with it.

3.35.oldText: Everything was so still that he imagined his aunt must be asleep, and crept silently through the house. On the threshold of the sitting room he stopped, breath held, preparing to approach Edele's door. The sitting room was flooded with sunshine, and a blossoming oleander made the air heavy with its sweet fragrance. There was no sound but a muffled splash from the flower-stand whenever the goldfish moved in their glass dish.

3.36.oldText: Niels crossed the room, balancing himself with outstretched arms, his tongue between his teeth. Cautiously he grasped the doorknob, which was so hot with the sun that it burned his hand, and turned it slowly and carefully, knitting his brows and half closing his eyes. He pulled the door toward him, bent in through the narrow opening, and laid the flowers on a chair just inside. The room was dark, as if the shades were drawn, and the air seemed moist with fragrance — the fragrance of attar of roses. As he stooped, he saw only the pale straw matting on the floor, the wainscoting beneath the window, and the lacquered foot of a small round table. But when he straightened up to back out of the door, he caught sight of his aunt.

3.37.oldText: She was stretched full-length on a couch of sea-green satin, dressed in a fanciful gypsy costume. She lay on her back, chin up, throat tense, and forehead low; her loosened hair flowed down over the end of the couch and along the rug. An artificial pomegranate flower looked as if it had been washed ashore on an island made by a small bronze-colored shoe in the midst of the dull golden stream.

3.38.oldText: The motley colors of her dress were rich and mellow. Dull blue, pale rose, grey, and orange were blended into the pattern of a low-cut little bodice of a thick, lustreless stuff. Underneath, she wore a white silk chemise with wide sleeves falling to the elbow. The white had a faint pinkish tone and was shot with threads of reddish gold. Her pansy-colored velvet skirt, without any border, was gathered loosely around her and slid down over the side of the couch in slanting folds. Her feet and legs were bare, and around her crossed ankles she had wound a necklace of pale corals. An open fan lay on the floor, showing its pattern of playing cards arranged in a wheel, and a little farther off a pair of leaf-brown silk stockings had been thrown down — one partly rolled up, the other spread out and revealing the red clock.

3.39.oldText: At the same moment Niels caught sight of her, she saw him. Involuntarily she made a slight movement, as if to rise, but checked herself and lay still as before, only turning her head a little to look at the boy with a questioning smile.

3.40.oldText: "I brought these," he said, and went over to her with the flowers.

3.41.oldText: She held out her hand, glanced at them and then at her costume, comparing the colors, and let them drop with a wearily murmured "Impossible!"

3.42.oldText: Niels would have picked them up, but she stopped him with a gesture of her hand.

3.43.oldText: "Give me that!" she said, pointing to a red flask lying on a crumpled handkerchief at her feet.

3.44.oldText: Niels went to take it. His face was crimson as he bent over the milk-white, gently rounded legs and the long, slender feet, which had almost the intelligence of a hand in their fine, flexible curves. He felt dizzy, and when one foot suddenly turned and bent downward with a quick movement, he almost fell.

3.45.oldText: "Where did you pick the flowers?" Edele asked.

3.46.oldText: Niels pulled himself together and turned toward her. "I picked them in the pastor's rye field," he said, in a voice that sounded strange to himself. He handed her the flask without looking up.

3.47.oldText: Edele noticed his emotion and looked at him, astonished. Suddenly she blushed, raised herself on one arm, and drew her feet under her skirt. "Go, go, go, go!" she said, half peevishly, half shyly, and at every word she sprayed him with the attar of roses.

3.48.oldText: Niels went. When he was out of the room, she let her feet slide slowly down from the couch and looked at them curiously.

3.49.oldText: Running with unsteady steps, he hurried through the house to his own room. He felt quite stunned — there was a strange weakness in his knees and a choking sensation in his throat. He threw himself down on the couch and closed his eyes, but it was no use; a strange restlessness possessed him, his breath came heavily as in fear, and the light tortured him in spite of his closed eyelids.

3.50.oldText: Little by little, a change came over him. A hot, heavy breath seemed to blow on him and make him helplessly weak. He felt like someone in a dream who hears somebody calling and tries to go, but cannot move a foot, and is tortured by his weakness, sickening with the longing to get away, lashed to madness by that calling which does not know he is bound. And he sighed impatiently, as if he were ill, and looked around, quite lost. Never had he felt so miserable, so lonely, so forsaken, so forlorn.

3.51.oldText: He sat down in the flood of sunlight from the window, and wept.

3.52.oldText: From that day on, Niels felt a timid happiness in Edele's presence. She was no longer a human being like anyone else, but an exalted creature, divine by virtue of her strange, mystic beauty. His heart throbbed with rapture merely at the sight of her, kneeling to her in his heart, crawling to her feet in abject self-effacement. Yet there were moments when his adoration had to find vent in outward signs of submission. At such times he would lie in wait for a chance to slip into Edele's room and perform a fixed rite of a certain interminable number of kisses lavished on the little rug in front of her bed, her shoe, or any other object that offered itself to his idolatry.

3.53.oldText: He regarded it as a great piece of good fortune that his Sunday jacket happened, just then, to have been demoted to everyday use — for the lingering scent of attar of roses was like a mighty talisman by which he could conjure up in a magic mirror the image of Edele as he had seen her lying on the green couch in her masquerade costume. In the story he and Frithjof were telling each other, this image was ever present, and from now on the wretched Frithjof was never safe from barefoot princesses. If he dragged himself through the dense primeval forest, they would call to him from hammocks of vines. If he sought shelter from the storm in a mountain cave, they would rise from their couches of velvety moss to welcome him, and when he burst, bloody and smoke-blackened, into the pirate's cabin, shivering the door with a tremendous blow of his saber, he found them there too, reclining on the captain's green sofa. They bored him terribly, and he could not see why they should suddenly have become so necessary to their beloved heroes.

3.55.oldText: No matter how exalted a place a human being may set his throne, no matter how firmly he may press the tiara of the exceptional — that is, genius — upon his brow, he can never be sure that he may not, like Nebuchadnezzar, be seized with a sudden desire to go on all fours, to eat grass, and to herd with the common beasts of the field.

3.56.oldText: That was what happened to Mr. Bigum when he quite simply fell in love with Miss Edele; and it availed him nothing that he distorted history to find an excuse for his love by calling Edele Beatrice or Laura or Vittoria Colonna, for all the artificial halos with which he tried to crown his love were blown out as fast as he could light them by the stubborn fact that it was Edele's beauty he was in love with. Nor was it the graces of her mind and heart that had captivated him, but her elegance, her air of fashion, her easy assurance, even her graceful insolence. It was a kind of love that might well fill him with shamed astonishment at the inconstancy of the children of men.

3.57.oldText: And what did any of it matter! Those eternal truths and makeshift lies that were woven ring into ring to form the heavy armor he called his principles — what were they against his love? If they really were the strength and marrow and kernel of life, then let them show their strength; if they were weaker, let them break; if stronger — But they were already broken, picked apart like the mesh of rotten threads they were. What did she care about eternal truths? And the mighty visions — how would they help him? Thoughts that plumbed the unfathomable — could they win her? All that he possessed was worthless. Even if his soul shone with the radiance of a hundred suns, what use was it, when his light was hidden beneath the ugly sackcloth of a Diogenes' mantle? Oh, for beauty! Take my soul and give me my thirty pieces of silver — Alcibiades' body, Don Juan's mantle, and the rank of court chamberlain!

3.58.oldText: But, alas, he had none of these graces, and Edele was by no means attracted to his heavy, philosophic nature. His habit of seeing life in barbarously naked abstractions gave him a noisy dogmatism, an unpleasant positiveness that jarred on her like a misplaced drum in a concert of soft music. The strained quality of his mind, which always seemed to tense its muscles and strike an attitude before every little question like a strongman about to juggle with iron balls, seemed to her ridiculous. He irritated her with his censorious morality, which pounced on every lightly sketched feeling, indiscreetly tearing off its incognito and rudely calling it by name just as it was about to flit past him in the course of conversation.

3.59.oldText: Bigum knew very well what an unfavorable impression he made, and how hopeless his love was — but he knew it as we know a thing when we hope with all the strength of our soul that our knowledge is false. There is always the miracle; and though miracles do not happen, they might happen. Who knows? Perhaps our intelligence, our instinct, our senses — in spite of their daylight clearness — are leading us astray. Perhaps the one thing needful is just that unreasoning courage which follows hope's will-o'-the-wisp as it burns over seething passions pregnant with desire! It is only when we have heard the door of destiny slam shut that we begin to feel the iron-cold talons of certainty digging into our breast, closing slowly, slowly around our heart, and fastening their clutches upon the fine thread of hope from which our world of happiness hangs: then the thread is severed; then all that it held falls and is shattered; then the shriek of despair sounds through the emptiness.

3.62.oldText: One sunny afternoon in September, Edele was sitting on the landing of the half-dozen broad, old-fashioned steps that led down from the summer parlor into the garden. Behind her, the French windows stood wide open, flung back against the motley wall-covering of bright red and bright green vines. She leaned her head against a chair piled high with large black portfolios, and held an etching up before her with both hands. Color prints of Byzantine mosaics in blue and gold were scattered over the pale green rush matting that covered the boards of the landing, on the threshold, and on the oak-brown parquet floor of the summer parlor. At the foot of the steps lay a white sun-hat, for Edele's hair was uncovered, adorned only by a flower of gold filigree in a pattern to match the gold bracelet she wore high on her arm. Her white dress was of semi-transparent stuff with narrow silky stripes; it had an edging of twisted orange and black chenille and tiny rosettes in the same two colors. Light silk mittens covered her hands and reached to the elbow. They were pearl grey, like her shoes.

3.63.oldText: The yellow sunlight was filtered through the drooping branches of an ancient ash. It pierced the cool dimness, forming distinct lines of light, powdering the air with gold dust, and painting the steps, the wall, and the doors with spots of light, sun-spot upon sun-spot, like a perforated shade. Through the tracery of shadow, each color rose to meet the light: white from Edele's dress, blood-red from crimson lips, amber from yellow-blonde hair, and a hundred other tints round about — blue and gold, oak-brown, glitter of glass, red and green.

3.64.oldText: Edele let the etching fall and looked up despondently, her eyes expressing the silent lament she was too weary to give vent to in a sigh. Then she settled down again as if to shut out her surroundings and withdraw into herself.

3.66.oldText: Edele looked at him with a drowsy blinking, like a child too sleepy and comfortable to stir but too curious to close its eyes.

3.67.oldText: Mr. Bigum wore his new beaver hat. He was absorbed in his own thoughts and gesticulated with his tombac watch in his hand until the thin silver chain threatened to snap. With a sudden, almost vicious movement, he thrust the watch deep into his pocket, threw back his head impatiently, caught the lapel of his coat in a peevish grasp, and would have gone on with an angry jerk of his whole body — his face darkened by all the hopeless rage that boils in a man when he is running away from his own torturing thoughts and knows that he runs in vain.

3.68.oldText: Edele's hat, lying at the foot of the steps and shining white against the black earth of the walk, stopped him in his flight. He picked it up with both hands, then caught sight of Edele, and as he stood trying to think of something to say, he held on to it instead of giving it to her. Not an idea could he find in his brain; not a word would be born on his tongue; and he stared straight ahead with a stupid expression of arrested profundity.

3.69.oldText: "It is a hat, Mr. Bigum," said Edele carelessly, to break the embarrassed silence.

3.70.oldText: "Yes," said the tutor eagerly, delighted to hear her confirm a likeness that had struck him too; but the next moment he blushed at his clumsy answer.

3.71.oldText: "It was lying here," he added hurriedly, "here on the ground like this — just like this," and he bent down to show where it had lain with an inconsequential minuteness born of his confusion. He felt almost happy in the relief of having given some sign of life, however futile. He was still standing with the hat in his hand.

3.72.oldText: "Do you intend to keep it?" asked Edele.

3.73.oldText: Bigum had no answer to that.

3.74.oldText: "I mean, will you give it to me?" she explained.

3.75.oldText: Bigum came a few steps nearer and handed her the hat. "Miss Lyhne," he said, "you think — you must not think — I beg you to let me speak; that is — I am not saying anything, but be patient with me! — I love you, Miss Lyhne, unutterably, unutterably, beyond all words I love you. Oh, if language held a word that combined the cringing admiration of the slave, the ecstatic smile of the martyr, and the gnawing homesickness of the exile, with that word I could tell you my love. Oh, listen to me — do not thrust me away yet! Do not think that I am insulting you with an insane hope! I know how insignificant I seem in your eyes, how clumsy and repulsive — yes, repulsive. I am not forgetting that I am poor — you must know it — so poor that I have to let my mother live in a charitable institution, and I cannot help it, cannot help it. I am so miserably poor. Yes, Miss Lyhne, I am only a poor servant in your brother's house, and yet there is a world where I am a ruler — powerful, proud, rich, crowned with victory, noble by virtue of the passion that drove Prometheus to steal fire from the heaven of the gods. There I am brother to all the great in spirit whom the earth has borne and who bear the earth. I understand them as only equals understand one another; no flight they have flown is too high for the strength of my wings. Do you understand me? Do you believe me? Oh, don't believe me! It isn't true — I am nothing but the kobold figure you see before you. It is all past; for this terrible madness of love has paralyzed my wings, the eyes of my spirit have lost their sight, my heart is dried up, my soul is drained to bloodless cowardice. Oh, save me from myself, Miss Lyhne, do not turn away in scorn! Weep over me, weep — it is Rome burning!"

3.76.oldText: He had fallen to his knees on the steps, wringing his hands. His face was blanched and distorted, his teeth clenched in agony, his eyes drowned in tears; his whole body shook under the suppressed sobs that were heard only as a gasping for breath.

3.77.oldText: "Control yourself, Mr. Bigum," she said, in a slightly too compassionate tone. "Control yourself; don't give way so — be a man! Please get up and go down into the garden a little while and try to pull yourself together."

3.78.oldText: "And you cannot love me at all?" groaned Mr. Bigum, almost inaudibly. "Oh, it is terrible! There is not a thing in my soul that I would not murder and degrade if I could win you by doing so. No, no — even if someone offered me madness, and I could possess you in my hallucinations, possess you, then I would say: Take my brain, tear down its wonderful structure with rude hands, break every fine thread that binds my spirit to the resplendent triumphal chariot of the human mind, and let me sink into the mire of the physical, under the wheels of the chariot, and let others follow the shining paths that lead to the light! Do you understand me? Can you comprehend that even if your love came to me robbed of its glory, debased, befouled, a caricature of love, a diseased phantom, I would receive it kneeling as if it were the Sacred Host? But the best in me is useless, the worst in me is useless too. I cry to the sun, but it does not shine; to the statue, but it does not answer — answer! What is there to answer except that I suffer? No, these unutterable torments that rend my whole being down to its deepest roots, this anguish — it is nothing to you but an impertinence. You feel nothing but a little cold offense; in your heart you laugh scornfully at the poor tutor and his impossible passion."

3.79.oldText: "You do me an injustice, Mr. Bigum," said Edele, rising, while Mr. Bigum rose too. "I am not laughing. You ask me if there is no hope, and I answer: No, there is no hope. That is surely nothing to laugh at. But there is one thing I want to say to you. From the first moment you began to think of me, you must have known what my answer would be — and you did know it, didn't you? You knew it all along, and yet you have been lashing all your thoughts and desires toward a goal you knew you could not reach. I am not offended by your love, Mr. Bigum, but I condemn it. You have done what so many people do: they close their eyes to the realities and stop their ears when life cries 'No' to their wishes. They want to forget the deep chasm fate has placed between them and the object of their ardent longing. They want their dream to be fulfilled. But life takes no account of dreams. There is not a single obstacle that can be dreamed out of the world, and in the end we lie there weeping at the edge of the chasm, which has not changed and is just where it always was. But we have changed, for we have let our dreams goad all our thoughts and spur all our longings to the very highest tension. The chasm is no narrower, and everything in us cries out with longing to reach the other side, but no, always no, never anything else. If only we had kept watch on ourselves in time! But now it is too late — now we are unhappy."

3.80.oldText: She paused, almost as though she were waking from a trance. Her voice had been quiet, groping, as if she were speaking to herself, but now it hardened into a cold aloofness.

3.81.oldText: "I cannot help you, Mr. Bigum. You are nothing to me of what you wish to be. If that makes you unhappy, then you must be unhappy; if you suffer, you must suffer — there are always some who have to suffer. If you make a human being your god and the ruler of your fate, you must bow to the will of your divinity, but it is never wise to make yourself gods, or to give your soul over to another, for there are gods who will not step down from their pedestals. Be sensible, Mr. Bigum! Your god is so small and so little worthy of your worship; turn away from it and be happy with one of the daughters of the land."

3.82.oldText: With a faint little smile, she went in through the summer parlor, while Mr. Bigum looked after her, crestfallen. For another quarter of an hour he walked up and down before the steps. All the words that had been spoken still seemed to be vibrating through the air; she had gone so recently, it seemed that her shadow must still linger there; it seemed she could not yet be beyond the reach of his prayers, and that everything could not be inexorably ended. But after a while the chambermaid came out and gathered up the engravings, carried in the chair, the portfolios, the rush matting — everything.

3.84.oldText: Up in the open gable window above, Niels sat gazing after him. He had heard the whole conversation from beginning to end. His face wore a frightened look, and a nervous trembling passed through his body. For the first time he was afraid of life. For the first time his mind grasped the fact that when life has sentenced you to suffer, the sentence is neither a fancy nor a threat, but you are dragged to the rack, and you are tortured, and there is no marvelous rescue at the last moment, no waking as from a bad dream.

3.85.oldText: He felt it as a foreboding that struck him with terror.

3.87.oldText: Edele did not have a good autumn, and the winter drained her strength completely. Spring, when it came, found not one poor little life-germ it could warm and coax into growth; it found only a withering that no gentleness and no warmth could arrest or even delay. But it could at least pour a flood of light over the paling life and caress the ebbing strength with fragrant, balmy air, as the evening crimson slowly follows in the wake of dying day.

3.88.oldText: The end came in May, on a day flooded with sunshine — one of those days when the lark is never silent and you can almost see the rye grow. The great cherry trees outside her window were white with blossom — nosegays of snow, wreaths of snow, cupolas, arches, garlands, a fairy architecture against the bluest of skies.

3.89.oldText: She was very weak that day, and at the same time felt a strange sense of lightness. She knew what was coming, for that morning she had sent for Bigum and said good-bye to him.

3.90.oldText: Her uncle had come over from Copenhagen, and all that afternoon the handsome, white-haired man sat by her bedside with his hand folded between hers. He did not speak, but every now and then he would move his hand, and she would press it; she would look up, and he would smile at her. Her brother, too, was in the room, gave her medicine, and helped her in other ways.

3.91.oldText: She lay very still with closed eyes while familiar pictures from life over there flitted past her. Sorgenfri with its drooping birches, the red church at Lyngby standing on its foundation of graves, and the white country house with the stretch of sunken road leading down to the sea, where the paling was always green as if painted by the water — the images took shape before her, grew clear, melted away, and vanished. And other pictures came. There was Bredgade when the sun went down and the darkness closed in around the houses. There was the queer Copenhagen you found when you came in from the country in the forenoon, and how weird it seemed with its hurry and bustle in the sunlight, with the whitened window-panes and the streets smelling of fruit. There was something unreal about the houses in the strong light; the noise and rattle of wheels could not chase away the silence that seemed to enfold them. Then came the dim, quiet drawing room on autumn evenings, when she was dressed for the theatre and the others had not come down yet — the smell of incense, the wood fire from the stove lighting up the carpet — the rain whipping the windows — the horses stamping at the door — the melancholy cry of the mussel-vendors... and behind all this the theatre awaiting her with light and music and festive glow.

3.92.oldText: With such pictures the afternoon wore away.

3.93.oldText: Niels and his mother were in the parlor. Niels knelt by the sofa with his face pressed against its brown velvet and his hands clasped over his head. He wept and wailed aloud, giving himself up to his grief without any attempt at self-control. Mrs. Lyhne sat beside him. The hymnbook lay on the table in front of her, open at the hymns usually sung at funerals. Now and then she read a few verses, and sometimes she would bend down over her son to speak a word of soothing or chiding, but Niels would not be comforted, and she could not stop his weeping or the wild prayers born of his despair.

3.94.oldText: Presently Lyhne appeared at the door of the sickroom. He made no sign, but looked at them so solemnly that both rose and followed him in to his sister. He took them by the hand and led them to the bed. Edele looked up and gazed at each one in turn, while her lips moved for words. Then Lyhne took his wife over to the window and sat down there with her. Niels threw himself on his knees at the foot of the bed.

3.95.oldText: He wept softly and prayed with clasped hands, eagerly and incessantly, in a low, passionate whisper. He told God that he would not stop hoping. "I won't let You go, Lord, I won't let You go until You have said 'Yes'! You mustn't take her away from us; for You know how we love her — You mustn't, You mustn't! Oh, I can't say, 'Thy will be done,' for Your will is to let her die — but oh, let her live! I will thank You and obey You. I will do everything I know You want me to do. I'll be so good and never offend You, if You will only let her live! Do You hear, God? Oh, stop, stop, and make her well before it's too late! I will, I will — oh, what can I promise You? Oh, I'll thank You, never, never forget You; oh, but hear me! Don't You see she's dying, don't You see she's dying? Do You hear? Take Your hand away! I can't lose her, God, I can't! Let her live, won't You please, won't You please? Oh, it's wicked of You —"

3.96.oldText: Outside, beyond the window, the white blossoms flushed to pink in the light of the setting sun. Arch upon arch, the blossoming sprays built of their gossamer bloom a rose-castle, a vaulted choir of roses, and through this airy dome the azure sky shone with a softened twilight blue, while golden lights and lights of gold flaming to crimson shot like the rays of a nimbus from every garlanded line of the ethereal temple.

3.97.oldText: White and still, Edele lay there with the old man's hand between both of hers. Slowly she breathed out her life, breath by breath; fainter and fainter grew the rising of her breast; heavier and heavier fell the eyelids.

3.98.oldText: "My love to Copenhagen!" was her last low whisper.

3.99.oldText: But her last message was heard by no one. It did not come from her lips even as a breath — her message to him, the great artist whom she had secretly loved with her whole soul, but to whom she had been nothing, only a name his ear knew, only one unrecognized figure in the great admiring public.

3.100.oldText: The light faded into blue dusk, and her hands fell weakly apart. The shadows grew — shadows of night and of death.

3.101.oldText: The old man bent down over her bed and laid his hand on her pulse, waiting quietly, and when the last throb of life had ebbed away, when the last feeble pulse-beat was stilled, he lifted the pale hand to his lips.

4.0.oldText: There are those who can take up their grief and bear it — strong natures who feel their own powers through the very heaviness of their burden. Weaker people give themselves up to their sorrow passively, as they would submit to an illness; and like a sickness their sorrow pervades them, drinks itself into their innermost being and becomes part of them, is assimilated through a slow struggle, and finally loses itself in them as they return to perfect health.

4.1.oldText: But there are still others for whom sorrow is a violence done to them, a cruelty they never learn to accept as a trial or a chastisement or as simple fate. To them it is an act of tyranny, an expression of personal hatred, and it always leaves a sting in their hearts.

4.2.oldText: Children do not often grieve in this way, but Niels Lyhne did. For had he not come face to face with God in the fervor of his prayers? Had he not crawled on his knees to the foot of the throne, full of hope, trembling with fear, and yet firm in his faith in the omnipotence of prayer, with courage to plead until he should be heard? And he had been forced to rise from the dust and go away with his hope put to shame. His faith had not been able to bring the miracle down from heaven; no God had answered his cry; death had marched straight on and seized its prey, as if no sheltering wall of prayers had been raised toward the sky.

4.3.oldText: A stillness came over him. His faith had flung itself blindly against the gates of heaven, and now it lay on Edele's grave with broken wings. For he had believed with the crude, implicit fairy-tale faith that children so often feel. The complex, subtly shaded figure of the Catechism is not the God children believe in; their God is the mighty one of the Old Testament — He who loved Adam and Eve so much, and to whom the whole generation of men, kings, prophets, and Pharaohs, are nothing but good and bad children. That tremendous, fatherly God, who is wrathful with the anger of a giant and bountiful with the generosity of a giant, who has hardly created life before He looses death upon it, who drowns His earth in the waters from His heaven, who thunders down laws too heavy for the race He made, and who, at last, in the days of the Emperor Augustus, takes pity on men and sends His Son to death so that the law may be broken even as it is fulfilled. This God, who always answers with a miracle, is the one to whom children speak when they pray. By and by a day comes when they understand that they have heard His voice for the last time in the earthquake that shook Golgotha and opened the graves — and that now, since the veil of His Holy of Holies has been rent in two, it is the God Jesus who reigns; and from that day on they pray differently.

4.4.oldText: But Niels had not yet come to this. It is true that he had followed Jesus on His earthly pilgrimage with a believing heart, but when he saw Him submitting to the Father, going about so bereft of power and suffering so humanly, all this had hidden the godhead from him. He had seen in Him only the one who did the Father's will, the Son of God, not God Himself. And so it was to God the Father that he had prayed, and it was God the Father who had failed him in his bitterest need. But if God had turned from him, he could turn from God. If God had no ears, he had no lips; if God had no compassion, he had no worship; and he defied and cast God out of his heart.

4.5.oldText: On the day Edele was buried, he spurned the earth of the grave with his foot whenever the pastor spoke the name of the Lord, and when he met that name afterward in books or on the lips of people, a rebellious frown would wrinkle his youthful forehead. When he lay down to sleep at night, a sense of forsaken greatness would come over him as he thought that now all the others, children and grown people alike, were praying to the Lord and closing their eyes in His name, while he alone withheld his hands from clasping in prayer, he alone refused to do God homage. He was shut out from the sheltering care of Heaven. No angel watched beside him; alone and unprotected, he drifted on the strangely murmuring waters of darkness, and loneliness closed around him, spreading out from his bed in ever widening and receding circles. Still he did not pray; though he longed till the tears came, he did not call.

4.6.oldText: And so it was all his life. He had defiantly freed himself from the view imposed on him by his teachers, and he fled with his sympathy to the side of those who had wasted their strength in vainly kicking against the pricks. In the books he had been given to read and in what he had been taught, God and His chosen people and ideas marched on in an endless triumphal procession, and he had joined in the jubilant shouting, had exulted in the sense of being counted among the proud legions of the conqueror — for is not victory always righteous, and is not the victor a liberator, a reformer, a bringer of light?

4.7.oldText: But now the shouting had died down. Now he was silent, and he began to enter into the thoughts of the defeated and feel with the hearts of the vanquished. He understood that even when the prevailing cause is good, that which yields is not on that account evil. He went over to the losing side and told himself that this was finer and greater. The power of the victor he called mere brute force and violence. He took sides — as wholeheartedly as he could — against God, but as a vassal who takes up arms against his liege lord; for he still believed, and could not drive out his faith by defiance.

4.8.oldText: His tutor, Mr. Bigum, was not a man who could lead a soul back to the old paths. Indeed, his temperamental philosophy, by virtue of which he could be fired and enraptured by each and every side of a question — today one, tomorrow another — set all dogmas adrift in the minds of his pupils. At bottom he was really a man of Christian principles, and if anyone could have pinned him down to say what was the fixed point in all this fluid matter, he would most likely have answered that it was the creed of the Evangelical Lutheran Church or something akin to it. But he himself had very little inclination to drive his pupils along the straight road of orthodoxy, or to warn them at every step that the least deviation from the beaten track meant straying into lies and darkness, likely to end in perdition and hell — for he had none of the orthodox's passionate concern for jots and tittles. He was, in fact, religious in the slightly artistic, superior manner that such talented people affect: not afraid of a little harmonizing, easily enticed into half-unconscious rearrangements and adaptations, because, whatever they do, they must assert their own personality, and in whatever spheres they fly must hear the whirring of their own wings.

4.9.oldText: Such people do not guide, but their instruction has a fullness, a copiousness, and a wobbly many-sidedness which — provided it does not utterly confuse the pupil — tends to develop his independence to a high degree, since it almost forces him to make up his own mind. For children can never rest on anything vague or indefinite; their very instinct of self-preservation demands a plain Yes or a plain No, a for or against, to show them where to turn with their hatred and where with their love.

4.10.oldText: And so there was no firm and immutable authority to guide Niels by constant clinching of arguments and pointing of ways. He had taken the bit between his teeth and plunged headlong down any path that opened before him, provided only that it led him away from what had been the home of his feelings and his thoughts.

4.11.oldText: He felt a new sense of power in thus seeing with his own eyes, choosing with his own heart, and forming himself by his own will. Many new things came to his mind; traits of his own nature that he had never thought of and that seemed unrelated to one another fitted themselves together wonderfully and were fused into a rational whole. It was a fascinating time of discovery. Little by little, in fear and uncertain exultation, in incredulous joy, he found himself. He began to realize that he was not like others, and a new spiritual modesty made him shy, awkward, and taciturn. He grew suspicious of questions and imagined he found hints of his own most hidden thoughts in everything that was said. Having learned to read in his own heart, he supposed everyone else could read what was written there, and he shunned his elders, preferring to roam about alone. It seemed to him that people had suddenly become very intrusive; he developed a slightly hostile feeling toward them, as toward creatures of another race, and in his loneliness he began to hold them up for scrutiny and judgment. Before, the names father, mother, the pastor, the miller, had been enough to characterize them, and the name had quite hidden the person from him. But now he saw that the pastor was a jolly little man who made himself as meek and demure as he could at home, to escape the notice of his wife, while away from home he tried to forget the domestic yoke by talking himself into a frenzy of rebellion and loud-voiced thirst for liberty. That was the pastor as he saw him now.

4.13.oldText: He had seen him ready to throw everything overboard for Edele's love, had heard him deny himself and the soul within him in that hour of passion in the garden — and now he was always talking about the philosopher rising in Olympian calm above the vague whirlwinds and mist-born rainbows of life. It roused a painful contempt in the lad and made his doubts sleep but lightly, ready to wake in a moment. For how could he know that the very things in human nature which Mr. Bigum called by belittling names were otherwise christened when they appeared in himself, and that his Olympian calm toward what moves common mortals was but a Titan's disdainful smile, quick with memories of a Titan's longing and a Titan's passions.

5.0.oldText: Six months had passed since Edele's death when one of Lyhne's cousins, Mrs. Refstrup, became a widow. Her husband had been a potter, but the business had never been flourishing, and during his long illness it had quite run to seed, so there was scarcely anything between the widow and actual want. Seven children were more than she could provide for. The two youngest and the eldest, who could help her at the factory, stayed with her, but the others were distributed among the family. The Lyhnes took the second boy, Erik, who was fourteen and had been studying at the Latin school in the nearest town, where he had free tuition. Now he was to share Mr. Bigum's instruction with Niels and Frithjof Petersen, the pastor's boy.

5.1.oldText: It was very much against his will that he was kept at his books, for he wanted to be a sculptor. His father had called it nonsense, but Lyhne had nothing against it; he said the boy had talent. Still, he thought he ought to take his bachelor's degree first, in order to have something to fall back on — and besides, a classical education was necessary to a sculptor, or was, at the very least, highly desirable. That settled the matter for the time being. Erik had to console himself with the fairly large collection of good engravings and neat bronzes that Lönborggaard had to offer. This meant a great deal to one who had seen nothing but the rubbish bequeathed to the local library by a bone-carver more freakish than artistic in taste, and Erik was soon busy with pencil and modeling-stick. No one attracted him as Guido Reni did — in those days more famous than Raphael and reckoned the greatest; nor is there anything that can open young eyes to the beauty of a work of art more surely than the certainty that one's admiration is authorized at the very highest level. Andrea del Sarto, Parmigianino, and Luini, who were to mean so much to him later when he and his talent had found each other, left him quite indifferent, while the boldness of Tintoretto and the bitterness of Salvator Rosa and Caravaggio filled him with delight. For sweetness in art has no appeal for the very young; the daintiest of miniature painters begins his career in the footsteps of Buonarotti, and the pleasantest of lyricists sets out on his first voyage under the black sail of bloody tragedy.

5.2.oldText: Still, Erik's art was to him only a game — only a little better than other games — and he was no more proud of a well-modeled head or a cleverly carved horse than of hitting the weather vane on the church steeple with a stone, or of swimming out to Sönderhagen and back without resting. Those were the games in which he excelled: games requiring physical prowess, strength, endurance, a sure hand, and a practised eye. He cared nothing for the kind of sport Niels and Frithjof liked, where fancy plays the leading role and all the events and triumphs are imagined. The result was that the other two soon dropped their old pastime to follow Erik's lead. Their romance books were laid aside, and the interminable story came to a rather violent end one day at a secret session in the hayloft. Silence brooded over its newly filled grave. In fact, they shrank from mentioning it to Erik at all, for he had not been with them many days before they suspected that he would make fun of them and their story, that he would shame them and lower them in their own eyes. He had the power to do it because he himself was so free from all daydreams and fancies and enthusiasms. His clear, boyish common sense was as merciless in its perfect healthfulness, and as contemptuous of mental idiosyncrasies, as children generally are of physical blemishes. For that reason Niels and Frithjof were afraid of him. They formed themselves after him, denied much and concealed more. Niels in particular was quick to suppress in himself anything that was not of Erik's world, and with the burning zeal of the renegade he scoffed at Frithjof, whose slower, more faithful nature could not instantly throw over the old for the new. His unkind mockery really sprang from jealousy, for he had fallen in love with Erik on the very first day, while Erik, in shy aloofness — half reluctant, half supercilious — just barely and grudgingly allowed himself to be loved.

5.3.oldText: Among all the emotional relations of life, is there any that is finer, more sensitive, and more fervent than the exquisitely modest love of one boy for another? It is a love that never speaks and never dares to vent itself in a caress or a look, a seeing love that grieves bitterly over every fault in the loved one, a love made up of longing and admiration and self-forgetfulness, of pride and humility and calmly breathing happiness.

5.4.oldText: Erik stayed at Lönborggaard only a little over a year. It happened that Lyhne, on a visit to Copenhagen, took the opportunity of speaking about the boy to one of the leading sculptors there, and showed him some of Erik's sketches — whereupon Mikkelsen, the sculptor, declared this was talent, and that further studying was a waste of time. It did not require much classical education to find a Greek name for a nude figure. So it was settled that Erik would be sent at once to the city to attend the Academy and work in Mikkelsen's studio.

5.5.oldText: On the last afternoon, Niels and Erik were sitting in their room — Niels looking at the pictures in a penny magazine, Erik deep in Spengler's critical catalogue of the art collection at Christiansborg. How often he had turned the leaves of this book and tried to form a conception of the pictures from its naïve descriptions! Sometimes he would grow almost sick with longing to behold all this art and beauty with his own eyes, to grasp it in truth and make that glory of line and color his own by the sheer strength of his enthusiasm. And how often, too, he had closed the book, weary of gazing into that drifting, fantastic mist of words which refused to solidify and take shape, refused to yield anything, but went on in a vague and confused shifting — flowing and slipping away — flowing and slipping away.

5.6.oldText: But today it was all different. Now he had the certainty that the shapes he read about would not be shadows from dreamland much longer, and he felt rich in the promise of the book. The pictures rose before him as never before, flashing out like brilliant, many-colored suns from a mist that was golden and dancing with gold.

5.7.oldText: "What are you looking at?" he asked Niels.

5.8.oldText: Niels pointed to a portrait in his book, a picture of Lassen, the hero of the Second of April.

5.10.oldText: "Ugly! Why, he was a hero — would you call him ugly, too?" Niels turned the leaves back to the picture of a great poet.

5.11.oldText: "Awfully ugly!" replied Erik decisively, making a grimace. "What a nose! And look at the mouth, and the eyes, and those tufts around his head!"

5.12.oldText: Then Niels saw that he was ugly, and he fell silent. It had never occurred to him that greatness was not always cast in a mold of beauty.

5.13.oldText: "While I think of it," said Erik, closing his Spengler, "let me give you the key to the deck-house."

5.14.oldText: Niels would have brushed him aside gloomily, but Erik hung a small padlock key around his friend's neck on a broad piece of ribbon. "Shall we go down there?" he asked.

5.15.oldText: They went. They found Frithjof by the garden fence. He lay there eating green gooseberries, and had tears in his eyes because of the parting. Besides, he was hurt that the others had not looked him up, for though he generally came uninvited, he felt that such a day demanded a certain amount of formality. Without speaking, he held out a handful of berries to them, but they had had their favorite dishes for dinner and turned up their noses.

5.17.oldText: "Indigestible junk!" added Niels, looking disdainfully down at the proffered berries. "How can you eat it? Chuck the stuff — we're going down to the deck-house," and he pointed with his chin at the key, since his hands were in his pockets.

5.18.oldText: And so all three of them set off.

5.19.oldText: The deck-house was an old green-painted ship's cabin which had once been bought at a beach auction. It had been put up by the fjord and had served as a tool-house when the dam was being built, but now it was no longer in use. So the boys had taken possession of it, and had concealed in it their ships, bows and arrows, leaping-poles, and other treasures — particularly such forbidden but indispensable things as powder, tobacco, and matches.

5.20.oldText: Niels opened the door of the deck-house with an air of gloomy solemnity. They went in and fumbled about until they found their things in the dark corners of the empty bunks.

5.21.oldText: "You know what," said Erik, his head deep in a distant corner, "I'm going to blow mine up."

5.22.oldText: "Mine and Frithjof's too!" cried Niels with a grand, consecrating gesture.

5.23.oldText: "Not mine, by Joe!" exclaimed Frithjof. "Then what would we have to sail with when Erik's gone?"

5.24.oldText: "What indeed!" mocked Niels, turning away contemptuously.

5.25.oldText: Frithjof felt uncomfortable, but when the others had gone outside, he carefully moved his ship to a safer shelter.

5.26.oldText: Outside they quickly laid the powder in the ships, bedded in a nest of tarred oakum, set the sails, fixed the fuses, lighted them, and sprang back. Running along the beach, they signalled to the crews on board, loudly explaining to one another every chance turn of the ships as the result of the good captain's nautical skill. But the ships ran aground at the point without the desired explosion having taken place, and this gave Frithjof an opportunity nobly to sacrifice the wadding of his cap to the manufacture of new and better fuses.

5.27.oldText: With all sails set, the ships stood in toward the Sjaelland reef; the Britisher's huge frigates came heavily lurching in a closed ring, while the foam blew white around the black bows and the cannon mounted at the head filled the air with their harsh clamor. Nearer and nearer — glowing with red and blue, glittering with gold, the figureheads of the Albion and the Conqueror rose fathom-high. Grayish masses of sails hid the horizon; the smoke rolled out in great white clouds and drifted as a veiling mist low over the sun-bright glitter of the waves. Then the deck of Erik's ship was splintered with a feeble little puff; the oakum caught, a red blaze burst forth, and the nimble flames licked the shrouds and ran along the spars, ate their way smouldering along the bolt-rope, then shot like long flashes of lightning into the sails, while the burning canvas shriveled up, broke, and flew in large black flakes far out to sea. The Danebrog still waved high on the slender top of the tall schooner mast; the flagstaff burned in two, the flag fluttered wildly like red wings eager for battle — but the flame caught it, and the smoke-blackened ship drifted without rudder or helmsman, dead and powerless, the sport of winds and breakers. Niels's ship did not burn so well: the powder caught, and some smoke came out, but that was all, and it was not enough.

5.28.oldText: "Hey, there!" called Niels from the point. "Sink her! Point the starboard cannon down the aft hatch and give her a volley!" He bent down and picked up a stone. "Ready — fire!" And the stone flew from his hand.

5.29.oldText: Erik and Frithjof followed suit, and soon the hull was in splinters. Then Erik's ship met the same fate. The wreckage was hauled ashore to make a bonfire. It was piled up with dry seaweed and grass into a burning heap, from which thick smoke rose, while the crystals clinging to the seaweed burst and crackled with the intense heat.

5.30.oldText: For a long time the boys sat quietly around the bonfire, but suddenly Niels, still gloomy, jumped up, brought all his things from the deck-house, broke them into little bits, and threw them into the flames. Then Erik brought his, and Frithjof brought some too. The flames of the sacrificial pyre leaped so high that Erik was afraid they might be seen from the pasture, and he began to smother them with wet seaweed. But Niels stood still, gazing sorrowfully after the smoke that drifted along the beach.
