He knew that he could get down to the shore through the mangling-room. If anyone saw him, he meant to say that he had forgotten his mandolin down by the jetty and wanted to rescue it from the dew. Therefore he slung the mandolin on his back.

10.48.oldText: The garden was a little lighter now; there was a slight breeze and a bit of moon that laid a tremulous strip of silver from the jetty out to the Berendt Claudi.

10.49.oldText: He went through the garden out onto the stone sloping that protected it from the water, running in abrupt angles around a large embankment and all the way out to the end of the harbor mole. Balancing uncomfortably on the flat, slanting stones, he finally reached the molehead and, rather out of breath, sat down on the bench.

10.50.oldText: Above his head, the red lantern of the harbor light swung slowly back and forth with a sound like the sighing of iron, while the flag-line flapped gently against its staff.

10.51.oldText: The moon had come out a little more and cast a cautious grayish-white light over the quiet ships in the harbor and over the maze of rectangular roofs and white dark-eyed gables in the town. Above and beyond it all, the church steeple rose, calm and light.

10.52.oldText: He leaned back dreaming, while a wave of unutterable joy and exultation surged through his heart; he felt rich and full of strength and the warmth of life. It seemed as though Fennimore must hear every love-thought that grew from his rapture, vine after vine, blossom after blossom; and he rose, and quickly striking the strings of the mandolin sang triumphantly to the town asleep in there:

10.53.oldText: "Wakeful aloft lies my lassie, She listens to my song!"

10.54.oldText: Again and again, when his heart grew too full, he repeated the words of the old ballad.

10.55.oldText: Gradually he grew calmer. Memories of the hours in the past when he had felt weakest, poorest, and most forlorn pressed in on him with a slight, tense pain like that of the first tears welling up in the eyes. He sat down on the bench again, and with his hand lying mute on the mandolin strings, he gazed out over the blue-gray expanse of the fjord, where the moon bridge formed a glittering way past the dark ship to the lines of the Morsö hills, drawn in faint, melancholy cloud-blue land through a haze of white.

10.56.oldText: And the memories thronged, but they grew gentler, were lifted to fairer lands, and seemed lighted by a roseate dawn.

10.59.oldText: "Wakeful aloft lies my lassie, She listens to my song."

11.0.oldText: Three years had passed; Erik and Fennimore had been married for two years and made their home in a little villa at Mariagerfjord. Niels had not seen Fennimore since that summer at Fjordby. He lived in Copenhagen and went out a great deal, but he had no close friends except Dr. Hjerrild, who called himself old because touches of gray had begun to show in his dark hair.

11.1.oldText: That unexpected engagement had been a hard blow to Niels. It had a numbing effect on him. He grew more bitter and less open, and no longer had so much enthusiasm to set against Hjerrild’s pessimism. Though he still pursued his studies, their plan became less and less definite, while his intention of one day completing them and beginning his real life-work flickered uncertainly. He lived much among people but very little with them. They interested him, but he did not in the least care whether they were interested in him; for he felt the force that should have driven him to do his part with the others or against them slowly ebbing out of him. He could wait, he told himself, even if he had to wait till it was too late. Whoever has faith is in no hurry — that was his excuse to himself. For he believed that, when he came down to the bedrock of his own nature, he did have faith strong enough to move mountains; the trouble was only that he never managed to put his shoulder to them. Once in a while the impulse to create welled up in him, and he longed to see a part of himself set free in work that was truly his own. For days he would be excited with the happy, titanic effort of carting the clay for his Adam, but he never shaped it in his own image. The will-power needed for persistent self-concentration was not in him. Weeks would pass before he could bring himself to abandon the work, but he did abandon it, asking himself in irritation why he should go on. What more did he have to gain? He had tasted the rapture of conception; what remained was the toil of rearing, cherishing, nourishing, carrying to perfection — why? for whom? He was no pelican, he told himself. But argue as he might, he was dissatisfied with himself and felt that he had not fulfilled his own expectations; nor did it help to carp at these expectations and ask whether they were well founded. He had reached the point where he had to choose, for when first youth is past — early or late, depending on the individual — then, early or late, dawns the day when Resignation comes to us as a temptress, luring us to give up the impossible and be content. And Resignation has much in her favor; for how often have the idealistic aspirations of youth not been beaten back, its enthusiasms shamed, its hopes laid waste! The ideals, the fair and beautiful, have lost nothing of their radiance, but they no longer walk here among us as in the early days of our youth. The broad, firmly planted staircase of worldly wisdom has carried them back, step by step, up to that heaven from which our simpler faith once brought them down; and there they sit, radiant but distant, smiling but weary, in divine stillness, while the incense of a slothful adoration rises, puff on puff, in festive curls.

11.2.oldText: Niels Lyhne was tired. These repeated run-ups to a leap that was never leaped had worn him out. Everything seemed to him hollow and worthless, distorted and confused, and oh, so petty! He preferred to stop his ears and his mouth and bury himself in studies that had nothing to do with the busy everyday world but were like an ocean of their own, where he could wander peacefully in silent forests of seaweed among curious creatures.

11.3.oldText: He was tired, and the root of his weariness lay in his baffled hope of love; from there it had spread, quickly and surely, through his whole being, to all his faculties and all his thoughts. Now he was cold enough, and passionless enough, but in the beginning, after the blow had fallen, his love had grown day by day with the irresistible power of a malignant fever. There had been moments when his soul was almost bursting with insane passion; it swelled like a wave in its infinite longing and frothing desire; it rose and went on rising and rising, until every fibre in his brain and every cord in his heart was strung tight to the breaking-point. Then weariness had come, soothing and healing, making his nerves dull against pain, his blood too cold for enthusiasm, and his pulse too weak for action. And more than that, it had guarded him against a relapse by giving him all the caution and self-interest of the convalescent. When his thoughts went back to those days at Fjordby, he had a sense of immunity like that of a man who has just come through a severe illness and knows that now, having endured his allotted agony and with the fever burned to ashes within him, he will be free for a long, long time.

11.4.oldText: Then it happened, one summer day after Erik and Fennimore had been married for two years, that Niels received a half-whining, half-boasting letter from Erik, in which he blamed himself for having wasted his time of late. He did not know what was the matter, but he had no ideas. The people he met in the neighborhood were fine, jolly fellows, with no conventionality or nonsense about them, but when it came to art they were perfect dromedaries. There was not a soul he could talk with, and he had drifted into a slough of laziness and stagnation that he could not pull himself out of. He never had a glimmer of an idea or a mood, and never felt inspired. Sometimes he was afraid his power had run dry and that he would never do anything again. But this could not possibly go on forever! It must come back; he had been too rich to end like this, and when it did come he would show them what art was, those fellows who painted away all the time as if they had learned it by rote. For the moment, however, he was as if bewitched, and it would be an act of friendship if Niels would visit him at Mariagerfjord. They would make him as comfortable as circumstances allowed, and he could just as well spend his vacation there as anywhere else. Fennimore sent her love and would be glad to see him.

11.5.oldText: This letter was so unlike Erik that Niels saw at once that something serious must be wrong, or Erik would not complain in this fashion. He knew, too, how little reservoir lay behind the wellspring of Erik’s production — only a slender stream, which unfavorable circumstances could easily dry up. He would go at once! For all that had happened, Erik should find him a faithful friend; whatever the years had loosened of old ties and uprooted of old illusions, he would at least know how to guard this old friendship of their childhood. He had helped Erik before; he would help him now. A fanaticism of friendship possessed him. He would renounce his future, fame, ambitious dreams, everything, for Erik’s sake. All the smoldering enthusiasm and creative ferment he had in him should be Erik’s; he would merge himself into Erik with his whole being and all his ideas, holding nothing back, keeping nothing for himself. He dreamed of greatness for the friend who had torn his life apart so roughly, and saw himself blotted out, forgotten, impoverished, stripped of his intellectual inheritance; and he went on dreaming that his gift to Erik should become not a loan but Erik’s very own, as Erik coined it into works and deeds and stamped it with his own mark. Erik in honor and glory, and Niels himself one of the many, many commonplace folk and nothing more; poor at last by necessity, not by choice; a real beggar, not a prince in disguise.... And it was sweet to dream himself so bitterly humble.

11.6.oldText: But dreams are dreams, and he laughed at himself when he thought how people who neglect their own work always find endless time to interest themselves in the work of others. It also struck him that when he came face to face with Erik, Erik would, of course, disown his letter and pass it off as a joke. He would certainly think it utterly absurd if Niels actually turned up announcing that he was ready to help him recover his creative power. Nevertheless he went. In his heart of hearts he believed he could do some good, and however much he tried to explain it away or cast doubts upon it, he could not rid himself of the feeling that this really was their boyhood friendship reasserting itself in all its old simplicity and warmth, in spite of the years and what the years had brought.

11.8.oldText: The villa at Mariagerfjord belonged to an elderly couple who had been forced by ill-health to make their home in the south for an indefinite time. They had not intended to rent the place, since they had set off thinking they would return after six months, and so had left everything just as it was. So when Erik leased the house fully furnished, the phrase was literal: he got it with bric-à-brac, family portraits, and everything else, down to an attic full of decrepit furniture with old letters in the drawers of the secretaries.

11.9.oldText: Erik had discovered the villa when he left Fjordby after his engagement. Since it contained everything they needed, and since he hoped to go to Italy in a year or two, he had talked Consul Claudi into putting off the purchase of household furnishings for a while. They had moved into Marianelund much as one moves into a hotel, except that they brought a few more trunks than travellers usually carry.

11.10.oldText: The house faced the fjord, less than twenty feet from the water, and was rather ordinary in appearance. It had a balcony above, a veranda below, and at the back a young garden with trees no thicker than walking-sticks; but from the garden one could step straight into a magnificent piece of beech forest with heathery glades and wide clefts opening between banks of white clay — and that made up for many shortcomings.

11.11.oldText: This was Fennimore’s new home, and for a while it was as bright as happiness could make it, for they were both young and in love, strong and healthy, and without a care for their livelihood, either spiritual or material.

11.12.oldText: But every palace of joy that rises toward heaven has sand mixed into the earth on which it is founded, and the sand will collect and run away — slowly perhaps, imperceptibly perhaps — but it runs and runs, grain by grain.... And love? Even love is no rock, however much we may wish to believe it.

11.13.oldText: She loved him with her whole soul, with the hot, tremulous passion born of fear. He was to her much more than a god, much nearer — he was an idol, whom she worshipped without reason and without reserve.

11.14.oldText: His love was as strong as hers, but it lacked that fine, manly tenderness which protects the beloved against herself and watches over her dignity. Dimly he felt it as a duty, one that called to him sometimes in a faint, low voice, but he would not listen. She was too alluring in her blind love; her beauty, which had the provocative luxuriance and the humble seductiveness of a female slave, drew him into a passion that knew neither bounds nor mercy.

11.15.oldText: In the old myth about Amor, isn’t it told somewhere that he puts his hand over Psyche’s eyes before they fly away, rapturously, into the glowing night?

11.16.oldText: Poor Fennimore! If she could have been consumed by the fire of her own heart, he who should have guarded her would have fanned the flames; for he was like that drunken monarch who swung the incendiary torch, shouting with joy to see his imperial city burn, intoxicating himself with the sight of the leaping flames, until the ashes made him sober.

11.17.oldText: Poor Fennimore! She did not know that the hymn of joy can be sung so often that both melody and words are lost, and nothing remains but a twaddle of triviality. She did not know that the intoxication lifting us up today takes its strength from the wings of tomorrow; and when at last sobriety dawned, gray and heavy, she realized with a tremor that they had loved themselves down into a sweet contempt for themselves and each other — a sweet contempt that day by day lost its sweetness and became at last utterly bitter. They turned away from each other as far as they could; he, to dream about his betrayed ideal of lofty coldness and scornful grace; she, to gaze with longing despair at the dim, quiet shores of her girlhood days, now immeasurably far away. With each day that passed it seemed harder to bear; shame burned madly in her veins, and a suffocating disgust with herself made everything seem wretched and hopeless. There was a small unused room containing nothing but the trunks she had brought from home, and there she would often sit, hour after hour, until the sun sank over the world outside and filled the room with reddish light. There she tortured herself with thoughts sharper than thorns and scourged herself with words more stinging than whips, until she was stupefied with misery and tried to deaden her pain by throwing herself on the floor as something too full of corruption and dregs — a carrion of herself — too foul to be the seat of a soul. Her husband’s mistress! That thought was never out of her mind; with that she threw herself in the dust and trampled on herself; with that she barred every hope of renewal and turned every happy memory to stone.

11.18.oldText: Gradually a hard, brutal indifference came over her, and she ceased to despair, as she had long since ceased to hope. Her heaven had fallen, but she did not try to raise the vault again in her dreams. The earth was good enough for her, since she was only of earth, earthy. She did not hate Erik, nor did she draw away from him. No, she accepted his kisses; she despised herself too much to push them away, and besides, was she not his wife — his woman?

11.19.oldText: For Erik too the awakening was bitter, though his man’s prosaic common sense had warned him that some day it must come. When it really came, however, when love no longer gave balm for every sting, and the shining golden veil in which it had descended to earth for him had been blown away, he felt such a sinking of his spirits and such a sluggishness creeping over all his powers that he was angered and alarmed. Feverishly he turned to his work to assure himself that he had lost nothing beyond happiness, but art did not give him the answer he hoped for. He got hold of some unlucky ideas that he could do nothing with and yet could not bring himself to abandon. Though they refused to take shape, they kept teasing his mind, and prevented other ideas from breaking through or absorbing his energy. He grew despondent and dissatisfied and sank into a moody idleness, since work was so confoundedly perverse, and since, of course, he had only to wait for the spirit to move him again. But time passed; his talent remained barren, and here by the quiet fjord there was nothing that could fertilize it; nor were there any fellow artists whose triumphs could spur him on, either to emulation or to creative opposition.

11.20.oldText: This inactivity grew unbearable. He was seized by a violent craving to feel himself — no matter how, or in what — and since nothing else offered, he turned to a crowd of older and younger men about the neighborhood who enlivened the dullness of country life with such dissipations as their limited imagination could invent and their rather one-sided taste could enjoy. The kernel of their pleasures was always drinking and cards, no matter whether the shell enclosing them was called a market day or a hunt. Nor did it make much difference if the scene was occasionally laid in a small neighboring town, with certain real or imagined business transacted with the tradesmen during the afternoon; for the bargain was always closed at night in the tavern, where the discriminating landlord always showed persons of the right stripe into Number Caveat. If there happened to be strolling players in town, the tradesmen were dropped, for the players were more sociable, did not shy at the bottle, and were usually ready to attempt the miraculous — though never quite successful — cure of drinking themselves sober in gin after getting drunk on champagne.

11.21.oldText: The leader of the crowd was a hunting squire of sixty, and the main body was made up of small landowners and country gentlemen in the neighborhood, though it also included a massive young dandy of a brandy-distiller and a white-necked tutor who had not been a tutor for twenty years or more, but had gone as a vagrant from house to house with a sealskin bag and an old gray mare, which he used to say he had bought from a horse-butcher. He was a silent drinker, a virtuoso on the flute, and was supposed to know Arabic. Among those whom the squire called his “staff” were also a solicitor, who always had new stories to tell, and a doctor, who knew only a single one — from the siege of Lübeck in the year 6.

11.22.oldText: The members of this band were widely scattered, and it almost never happened that they were all together at one time, but whenever one of them stayed away from the company too long the squire would issue a summons to the faithful to inspect the renegade’s oxen, which all understood to mean that they should quarter themselves on the unfortunate man for two or three days and turn his house upside down with drinking, gambling, and whatever rustic amusements the season afforded. During one such punitive visit, the whole party was once snowbound, and the host’s supply of coffee, rum, and sugar ran out, so that they were reduced to drinking a coffee punch boiled from chicory, sweetened with syrup, and strengthened with brandy.

11.23.oldText: It was a coarse-grained crowd of boon companions that Erik had fallen in with, but perhaps people of such tremendous animal vitality could hardly find a sufficient outlet in more civilized amusements, and their unfailing good humor and broad, bearish joviality really took away much of the coarseness. If Erik’s talent had been akin to that of Brouwer or Ostade, this choice band of revellers would have been a perfect gold mine to him. As it was, he got nothing out of it except that he enjoyed it very much — too much, in fact, for soon this wild racketing became indispensable to him and took up nearly all his time. Now and then he would blame himself for his idling and vow to end it, but whenever he attempted to work, the sense of blankness and spiritual impotence came over him again and drove him back to the old life.

11.24.oldText: The letter to Niels had been written one day when his chronic barrenness had made him wonder whether his talent had been attacked by a wasting disease. As soon as it was sent, he regretted it, and hoped that Niels would let his plaint go in at one ear and out at the other.

11.25.oldText: But Niels came — the knight-errant of friendship personified — and was met with that mixture of rebuff and pity which knights-errant in every age have encountered from those for whose sake they have dragged Rosinante out of her snug stable. Since Niels was tactful, however, and bided his time, Erik thawed before long, and the old intimacy was soon established between them; for Erik’s need to pour himself out in complaint and confession had grown into an almost physical craving.

11.26.oldText: One evening after bedtime, when Fennimore had retired, they sat over their cognac and water in the dark sitting room. Only the glow of their cigars showed where they were, and once in a while, when Niels leaned far back in his chair, his upturned profile would stand out black against the dark windowpane. They had been drinking a good deal — Erik especially — as they sat talking of the days when they were boys at Lönborggaard. Now Fennimore’s leaving the room had made a pause which neither of them seemed inclined to break, for their thoughts came stealing upon them in a pleasant languor, as they listened drowsily to the singing of their blood, warm with the cognac.

11.27.oldText: “What fools we were at twenty,” came Erik’s voice at last. “God knows what we expected, or how we had got it into our heads that such things existed on earth. We called them by the same names they bear in reality, but we meant something altogether beyond comparison with this tame sufficiency we’ve got. There really isn’t much to life. Do you think there is?”

11.28.oldText: “Oh, I don’t know; I take it for what it’s worth. We don’t generally _live_ very much. Most of the time we only exist. If you could get life handed to you in one whole large, appetizing cake that you could set your teeth into ... but doled out in bits! — no, it isn’t amusing.”

11.29.oldText: “Tell me, Niels — you’re the only one I can talk to about such absurd things; I don’t know why, but you’re so queer. Tell me — is there anything in your glass? All right! — Have you ever thought about death?”

11.31.oldText: “I don’t mean at funerals or when a man is sick, but sometimes when I’m just sitting here comfortably it comes over me like — like a despair, simply. When I sit here and mope and don’t do anything and _can’t_ do anything, then I actually feel the time slipping away from me. Hours and weeks and months rush past with nothing in them, and I can’t nail them down with a piece of work. I don’t know if you understand what I mean, but I want to grip hold of them with something achieved. When I paint a picture, the time I use for it remains mine forever; it isn’t lost, even though it’s past. I get sick when I think of the days as they go — incessantly. And I _have_ nothing, or I can’t get at it. It’s torture! I sometimes work myself into such a rage that I have to get up and walk the floor and sing some idiotic thing to keep from crying, and then when I stop I am almost mad to think that the time has gone in the meantime, and is going while I think, and going and going. There is nothing more wretched than to be an artist. Here I am, strong and healthy; I have eyes to see; my blood is warm and red; my heart beats, and there’s nothing wrong with my head, and I _want_ to work, but I can’t. I am struggling and groping for something that eludes me, something that I can’t grasp even if I toil and sweat blood over it. What can a man do for inspiration or to get an idea? It’s all the same whether I concentrate or whether I go out and pretend I am not looking for anything — never, never anything except the sense that now Time is standing up to his waist in eternity and hauling in the hours, and they rush past, twelve white and twelve black, never stopping, never stopping. What shall I do? What do people do when they feel like that? Surely I can’t be the first. Have you nothing to suggest?”

11.33.oldText: “No, anything but that. What made you think of that? You don’t believe I’m done for, do you?”

11.34.oldText: “Done for! No, but I thought the new impressions —”

11.35.oldText: “The new impressions! Exactly. Have you never heard about people who had plenty of talent in their first youth, while they were fresh and full of hope and plans, but when youth had passed their talent was gone too — and never came back?”

11.36.oldText: They were silent for a long time.

11.37.oldText: “_They_ travelled, Niels, to get new impressions; that was their fixed idea. The south, the Orient — it was all in vain; it slid off them as off a looking-glass. I have seen their graves in Rome — two of them, but there are many, many others. One of them went mad.”

11.38.oldText: “I have never heard that about painters before.”

11.39.oldText: “It’s true. What can it be, do you think? A hidden nerve that’s given way? Or something we have failed in or sinned against in ourselves, perhaps — who knows? A soul is such a fragile thing, and no one knows how far the soul reaches in a human being. We ought to be good to ourselves — Niels!” His voice had grown low and soft. “I have often longed to travel, because I felt so empty. You have no idea how I have longed for it, but I simply don’t dare, for suppose it didn’t help, and I was one of those people I was telling you about. What then! Think of standing face to face with the certainty that I was done for, had nothing, could do nothing — think of it — could do nothing! A paltry wretch, a cursed dog of a cripple, a miserable eunuch! What do you think would become of me? And after all, it is not impossible. My first youth is past, and as for illusions and that sort of thing, I can assure you I haven’t many left. It’s terrible how we go through them, and yet I was never one of those who were anxious to be rid of them. I was not like you and the rest of the people who used to gather at Mrs. Boye’s — you were always so busy plucking the fine feathers from one another, and the balder you got, the more you crowed. Still, what’s the difference — sooner or later we all start molting.”

11.40.oldText: They were silent again. The air was bitter with cigar smoke and heavy with cognac, and they sighed drearily, oppressed by the stuffiness of the room and by their own very sad hearts.

11.41.oldText: Niels had travelled two hundred miles to bring help, and here he sat feeling his own impulse put to shame, while the colder side of his nature looked on. For what could he do, when it came to the point? What if he tried to talk picturesquely to Erik, in many words of purple and ultramarine, dripping with light and wading in shadow! A dream of something like that had been in his brain when he set out. How utterly absurd! To bring aid! You might perhaps drive the goddess with the closed hands from an artist’s door, but that was certainly the most; you could no more help him to create than you could help a paralyzed man to lift his little finger by his own strength. No, not though your heart overflowed with affection and sympathy and devotion and everything else that was generous.... What you ought to do was to mind your own affairs; that was useful and healthy, but of course it was easier to let your heart run amok in a large and generous way. The only trouble was that it was so lamentably impractical and so utterly ineffective. Minding your own affairs and doing it well did not guarantee you paradise, but at least you did not have to cast down your eyes before either God or man.

11.42.oldText: Opportunity was plentiful for Niels to make melancholy reflections on the impotence of a kind heart, for all he accomplished was to keep Erik at home a little more than usual for a month or so. Still, he did not care to return to Copenhagen during the hot season, and since he did not wish to remain a guest indefinitely, he rented a room with a family a little above the peasant class on the opposite shore of the fjord, so near that he could row over to Marianelund in fifteen minutes. Now that he was used to the neighborhood, he would just as soon stay there as anywhere else, for he was one of those susceptible people over whom outward surroundings easily acquire a hold. Besides, his friend and his cousin Fennimore were there, and that was reason enough, especially since there was no one anywhere else expecting him.

11.43.oldText: On the trip from Copenhagen he had carefully thought out how he would behave toward Fennimore and how he would show her that he had forgotten so completely that he did not even remember there was anything to forget; above all, no coldness, but a friendly indifference, a superficial cordiality, a polite sympathy — that was the proper attitude.

11.44.oldText: But it was all thrown away.

11.45.oldText: The Fennimore he met was a different person from the one he had left. She was still lovely; her figure was as luxuriant and beautiful as before, and she had the same slow, languid movements that had charmed him in former days, but there was a dreary thoughtlessness in the set of her mouth, like that of someone who has thought too much, and a pitiful, tortured cruelty in her gentle eyes. He did not understand it at all, but one thing at least was clear: she had had other things on her mind than remembering him, and she was quite callous to any memories he could awaken. She looked like someone who had made her choice and done the worst she could with it.

11.46.oldText: Little by little he began to spell things out and put them together, and one day, when they were walking along the shore, he began to understand.

11.47.oldText: Erik was cleaning up his studio, and as they were strolling by the water, the maid came out with an apronful of refuse, which she threw onto the beach. There was a litter of old brushes, fragments of casts, broken palette knives, bits of oil bottles, and empty paint tubes. Niels poked the heap with his foot, and Fennimore looked on with the vague curiosity people often feel in sifting through old rubbish. Suddenly Niels drew his foot away as if something had burned it, but caught himself just as quickly, and gave the pile another kick.

11.48.oldText: “Oh, let me see it,” begged Fennimore, and laid her hand on his arm as if to stop him. He bent down and pulled out a plaster cast of a hand holding an egg.

11.49.oldText: “It must be a mistake,” he said.

11.50.oldText: “Why no, it is broken,” she replied quietly, taking it from him. “See, the forefinger is gone,” she added, pointing; but when she suddenly noticed that the egg had been cut in two and a yolk painted inside it with chrome yellow, she blushed, and, bending down, slowly and deliberately knocked the hand against a stone until it was broken into little bits.

11.51.oldText: “Do you remember the time it was cast?” Niels asked, just to say something.

11.52.oldText: “I remember that my hand was smeared with green soap so the plaster wouldn’t stick to it. Is that what you meant?”

11.53.oldText: “No, I meant the time when Erik passed the cast around at the tea table. Don’t you remember, when it came to your old aunt, how her eyes filled with tears, and she embraced you with the deepest compassion and kissed you on the brow, as if some harm had been done to you?”

11.55.oldText: “No, we all laughed at her, but there was a delicacy in it nonetheless, absurd as it was.”

11.56.oldText: “Yes, there is a lot of that absurd delicacy in the world.”

11.57.oldText: “I think you’re looking for a quarrel with me today.”

11.58.oldText: “No, I’m not, but there is something I want to say to you. You won’t take offence at a little frankness? — Well, then — suppose a man tells a story that is not very nice in his wife’s presence, and perhaps shows in other ways what looks to you like a lack of consideration for her; don’t you think it is unnecessary for you then to express your protest by your emphatic fastidiousness and your exceeding great chivalry? It is fair to assume that the man knows his own wife best, and knows that it won’t offend or wound her; otherwise he would not do it. Isn’t that true?”

11.59.oldText: “No, as a general rule it isn’t true, but in this case, and on your authority, I don’t mind saying yes.”

11.60.oldText: “That’s right. You may be sure women are not the ethereal creatures many a good youth imagines; they’re really no more delicate than men, and not very different from them. Take my word for it, some filthy clay went into the shaping of both of them.”

11.61.oldText: “Dearest Fennimore! Thank God you don’t know what you are saying; but you are very unjust to women, and to yourself. _I_ believe in woman’s purity.”

11.62.oldText: “Woman’s purity! What do you mean by woman’s purity?”

11.64.oldText: “You mean — I’ll tell you; you mean nothing, for that is another piece of absurd delicacy. A woman can’t be pure, and isn’t supposed to be — how could she? It’s against nature! And do you think God made her to be pure? Answer me! — No, and ten thousand times no. Then why this lunacy! Why fling us up to the stars with one hand, when you have to pull us down with the other! Can’t you let us walk the earth by your side, one human being with another, and nothing more? It’s impossible for us to step firmly on the prose of life when you blind us with your poetic will-o’-the-wisps. Let us alone! For God’s sake, let us alone!”

11.66.oldText: Niels understood a great deal. Fennimore would have been miserable if she had known how much. Was it not partly the old story of love’s holiday fare, which refuses to turn into daily bread but keeps on being holiday fare — only more tasteless, more insipid, and less nourishing, day by day? One of them can’t perform a miracle, and the other can’t perform it either, and there they sit in their banquet clothes, careful to smile and to use festive words, but underneath they feel the agony of hunger and thirst, while their eyes shrink from each other, and hatred begins to grow in their hearts. Wasn’t that the first chapter, and wasn’t the other the equally dreary tale of a woman’s despair at not being able to recover herself after discovering that the demigod whose bride she had so joyously become was only an ordinary mortal? First the despair, the bootless despair, and then the merciful stupor — that must be the explanation. It seemed to Niels that he understood everything: the hardness in her, the dreary humility, and her coarseness, which was the bitterest drop in the whole goblet. Gradually he came to see as well that his delicacy and deferential homage must oppress and irritate her, because a woman who has been hurled from the purple couch of her dreams to the pavement below will quickly resent any attempt to spread carpets over the stones which she longs to feel in all their hardness. In her first despair she is not content to tread the path with her feet: she is determined to crawl it on her knees, choosing the way that is steepest and roughest. She wants no helping hand and will not lift her head — let it sink down with its own heaviness, so that she may put her face to the ground and taste the dust with her tongue!

11.67.oldText: Niels pitied her with all his heart, but he left her alone, as she wished.

11.68.oldText: It was hard to look on and not help, to sit apart and dream her happy, in foolish dreams, or to wait and calculate, with the cold knowledge of a physician, how long she still had to suffer. He told himself, in this dreary wisdom, that there could be no relief until her old hope in the fair, gleaming treasures of life had bled to death and a sluggish stream had entered her veins, making her dull enough to forget, blunt enough to accept, and at last, at last, coarse enough to rejoice in the thick atmosphere of a bliss many heavens lower than that which she had meekly hoped for and humbly prayed for wings to reach. — He was filled with disgust at everything in the world when he thought that she, to whom he had once knelt in adoration, had come to such a pass that she had been forced into a slave’s estate and stood at the gate shivering with cold, while he rode past on his high horse with the large coins of life jingling in his pocket.

11.69.oldText: One Sunday afternoon toward the end of August, Niels rowed across the fjord. Fennimore was at home alone when he came; he found her lying on a sofa in the corner room, and very miserable. Her breath came with that low, monotonous moaning that seems to give some relief from pain, and she said she had a frightful headache. There was no one to help her, for she had given the maid leave to go home to Hadsund, and soon afterwards someone had come and carried off Erik; she couldn’t understand where they had gone in the rain. Now she had been lying there for two hours trying to sleep, but it had been impossible — the pain was so bad. She had never had it before, and it had come on so suddenly — at dinnertime there had been nothing the matter. First it had been in the temples, and then it seemed to dig deeper and deeper and deeper; now it seemed to be behind her eyes — if only it was not something dangerous. She was not used to being ill, and was very frightened and unhappy.

11.70.oldText: Niels comforted her as well as he could, telling her to lie still, close her eyes, and not speak. He found a heavy shawl and wrapped it around her feet, fetched vinegar from the buffet, and made a cold compress, which he laid on her brow. Then he sat down quietly by the window and looked out at the rain.

11.71.oldText: From time to time he stole over to her on tiptoe and changed the compress without speaking, merely nodding to her as she looked up at him gratefully between his hands. Sometimes she wanted to speak, but he hushed her with a look, shaking his head, and returned to his seat.

11.73.oldText: One hour passed, and another, and she was still sleeping. Slowly one quarter slipped into the next, while the melancholy daylight faded, and the shadows in the room grew larger, as though they were growing out of the furniture and the walls. Outside the rain fell, evenly and steadily, blotting out every other sound with its low, incessant patter.

11.75.oldText: The fumes of vinegar and the vanilla scent of the heliotrope, mingling in a pungent odor like wine, filled the room. Warmed by their breath, the air covered the gray windowpanes with a dewy film, which grew denser as the evening cooled.

11.76.oldText: By this time he was far away in memories and dreams, though a part of his consciousness still kept watch over the sleeper and followed her sleep. Gradually, as the darkness pressed in, his fancy wearied of feeding these dreams that flickered up and died down, just as the soil gets tired of bringing forth the same crop again and again; and the dreams grew feebler, more sterile, stiffer, losing the luxuriant details that had twined about them like long shoots of clinging vines. His thoughts left the distance and came homing back. — How quiet everything was! Was it not as if they were together, he and she, on an island of silence rising above the monotonous sea of sound made by the soft patter of the rain? And their souls were still, calm and safe, while the future seemed to slumber in a cradle of peace.

11.77.oldText: Would that it might never wake, and that all might remain as now — no more happiness than that of peace, but neither any misery nor restless longing! Would that the present might close like a bud around itself, and that no spring would follow!

11.78.oldText: Fennimore called. She had been lying awake for some time, too happy to be free of pain to think of speaking. Now she wanted to get up and light the lamp, but Niels continued to play the physician, and made her lie still. It was not good for her to get up yet; he had matches and could easily find the lamp.

11.79.oldText: When he had lit it, he set it on the flower stand in the corner, where its milky white globe shone softly veiled by the delicate, sleeping leaves of an acacia. The room was just light enough for them to see each other’s face.

11.80.oldText: He sat down in front of her, and they spoke about the rain and said how lucky it was that Erik had taken his raincoat, and how wet poor Trine would be getting. Then their conversation came to a halt.

11.81.oldText: Fennimore’s thoughts were not quite awake yet, and in her weakness it seemed pleasant to lie there musing without speaking. Nor was Niels inclined to talk, for he was still under the spell of the afternoon’s long silence.

11.82.oldText: “Do you like this house?” Fennimore asked at last.

11.84.oldText: “Really? Do you remember the furniture at home?”

11.86.oldText: “You don’t know how I love it, and how I long for it sometimes. The things we have here don’t belong to us — they are only rented — and have no associations with anything, and we are not going to live with them any longer than we stay in this place. You may think it queer, but I assure you, I often feel lonely here among all these strange pieces of furniture that stand around so indifferent and stupid and take me for what I am without caring the least bit about me. And since I know they aren’t going with me — that they’ll just stay here and be rented by other people — I can’t get fond of them or interested in them as I should if I knew that my home would always be theirs, and that whatever came to me of good or ill would come in their midst. Do you think it’s childish? Perhaps it is, but I can’t help it.”

11.87.oldText: “I don’t know what it is, but I have felt it too. When I was left alone abroad, my watch stopped, and when it came back from the watchmaker and was going as before, it was — just what you mean. I liked the feeling; there was something peculiar about it, something really good.”

11.88.oldText: “Yes indeed! Oh, I should have kissed it, if I had been you.”

11.90.oldText: “Do you know,” she said suddenly, “you have never told me anything about Erik as a boy? What was he like?”

11.91.oldText: “Everything that is good and fine, Fennimore. Splendid, brave — a boy’s ideal of a boy, not exactly a mother’s or a teacher’s ideal, but the other, which is so much better.”

11.92.oldText: “How did you get along together? Were you very fond of each other?”

11.93.oldText: “Yes, I was in love with him, and he didn’t mind — that is about how it was. We were very different. I always wanted to be a poet and become famous, but what do you suppose he said he wanted to be, one day when I asked him? — An Indian, a real red Indian with war paint and all the rest! I remember that I couldn’t understand it at all. It was incomprehensible to me how anyone could want to be a savage — civilized creature that I was!”

11.94.oldText: “But wasn’t it strange, then, that he should become an artist?” said Fennimore, and there was something cold and hostile in her tone as she asked.

11.95.oldText: Niels noticed it with a little start. “Not at all,” he answered; “it is really rare for people to become artists with the whole of their nature. And such strong fellows overflowing with vitality like Erik often have an unutterable longing for what is fine-grained and delicate: for an exquisite virginal coldness, a lofty sweetness — I hardly know how to put it. Outwardly they may be robust and full-blooded enough, even coarse, and no one suspects what strange, romantic, sentimental secrets they carry around with them, because they are so bashful — spiritually bashful, I mean — that no pale little maiden can be more shy about her soul than are these big, hard-stepping menfolk. Don’t you understand, Fennimore, that such a secret, which can’t be put into plain words out in ordinary everyday air, may dispose a man to be an artist? And they can’t express it in words; they simply can’t; we have to believe that it is there and lives its quiet life within them, as the bulb lives in the earth; for once in a while they do send fragrant, delicately tinted flowers up into the light. Do you understand? — Don’t demand anything for yourself out of this blossoming strength; believe in it, be glad to nourish it and to know it is there. — Forgive me, Fennimore, but it seems to me that you and Erik are not really good to each other. Can’t you make a change? Don’t think about who is right or how great the wrong is, and don’t treat him according to his deserts — how would even the best of us fare if we got our deserts! No, think of him as he was in the hour when you loved him most; believe me, he is worthy of it. You must not measure and weigh. There are moments in love, I know, full of bright, solemn ecstasy, when we would give our lives for the beloved if need be. Isn’t that true? Remember it now, Fennimore, for his sake and your own.”

11.97.oldText: She said nothing either, but lay very still with a melancholy smile on her lips, pale as a flower.

11.98.oldText: Then she half rose and stretched out her hand to Niels. “Will you be my friend?” she asked.

11.99.oldText: “I am your friend, Fennimore,” and he took her hand.

11.101.oldText: “Always,” he replied, lifting the hand to his lips reverently.

11.102.oldText: When he rose, it seemed to Fennimore that he held himself more erect than she had ever seen him before.

11.103.oldText: A little later Trine came in to announce her return, and then there was tea, and at last the rowing back through the dreary rain.

11.104.oldText: Toward morning Erik came home, and when Fennimore saw him by the cold, truthful light of dawn, preparing to go to bed, heavy and unsteady with drink, his eyes glazed from gambling and his face dirty-pale after the sleepless night, then all the fair words Niels had spoken seemed to her quite visionary. The bright promises she had made to her own heart fainted and paled before the oncoming day — vapory dreams and fumes of fancy: a fairy flock of lies!

11.105.oldText: What was the use of struggling with this weight dragging them both down? It was futile to lighten it with lies; their life would never have its old buoyancy again. The frost had come, and the wealth of vines and creepers and clustering roses and blossoms fairer than roses that had twined around them had shed every tiny leaf, lost every blossom, and nothing remained but the tough, naked withes tying them together in an unbreakable tether. What good did it do that she roused the feelings of former days to an artificial life by the warmth of memories, that she set her idol back on its pedestal, that she called the light of admiration back into her eyes, the words of adoration to her lips, and the flush of happiness to her cheeks? What good did any of it do when he would not take it on himself to be the priest of the idol and so help her to a pious fraud? He! He did not even remember her love. Not one of her words echoed in his ears, not one of all their days was hidden in his soul.

11.106.oldText: No, dead and cold was the ardent love of their hearts. The fragrance, the glamor, and the tremulous notes — all had been blown away. There they sat, from force of habit, he with his arm around her waist, she with her head resting on his shoulder, drearily sunk in silence, forgetting each other; she, to remember the glorious hero he had never been; he, to transform her in his dreams into the ideal he now always saw shining in the sky high above her head. Such was their life together, and the days came and went without bringing any change, and day after day they gazed out over the desert of their lives, and told themselves that it was a desert, that there were no flowers, nor any hope of flowers or springs or green palms.

11.107.oldText: As the autumn wore on, Erik’s drinking-bouts became more frequent. What was the use, he said to Niels, of sitting at home waiting for ideas that never came, until his thoughts turned to stone in his head? Moreover, he didn’t get much comfort from Niels’s company; he needed people with some grit in them, people of lusty flesh and blood, not a whim-wham of delicate nerves. Niels and Fennimore were therefore left much alone, for Niels came over to Marianelund every day.

11.108.oldText: The covenant of friendship they had made and the talk they had had on that Sunday afternoon put them at ease with each other, and, lonely as they both were, they drew closer together in a warm and tender friendship, which soon gained a strong hold over both of them. It absorbed them so that their thoughts, whether they were together or apart, always turned back to this bond, as birds building the same nest look at everything they gather or pass by with the one pleasant goal of making the nest snug and comfortable for each other and themselves.

11.109.oldText: If Niels came while Erik was away, they nearly always, even on rainy and stormy days, took long walks in the woods behind the garden. They had fallen in love with that forest, and grew fonder of it as they watched the summer life die out. There were a thousand things to see. First, how the leaves turned yellow and red and brown, then how they fell off, whirling on a windy day in yellow swarms, or softly rustling in still air, single leaf after single leaf, down against the stiff boughs and between the pliant brown twigs. And when the leaves fell from trees and bushes, the hidden secrets of summer were revealed in nest after nest. What treasures on the ground and on the branches — dainty seeds and bright-colored berries, brown nuts, shining acorns and exquisite acorn cups, tassels of coral on the barberry, polished black berries on the buckthorn, and scarlet urns on the dog-rose. The bare beeches were finely dotted with prickly beechnuts, and the rowan bent under the weight of its red clusters, acid in fragrance like apple cider. Late brambleberries lay black and brown among the wet leaves at the wayside; red whortleberries grew among the heather, and the wild raspberries put forth their dull crimson fruit for the second time. The ferns turned all colors as they faded, and the moss was a revelation — not only the deep, luscious moss in the hollows and on the slopes, but the faint, delicate growth on the tree-trunks, resembling what one might imagine the cornfields of the elves to be as it sent forth the finest of stalks with dark brown buds like ears of corn at the tip.

11.110.oldText: They scoured the forest from end to end, eager to find all its treasures and marvels. They had divided it between them as children do; the part on one side of the road was Fennimore’s property, and that on the other side was Niels’s, and they would compare their realms and quarrel over which was the more glorious. Everything there had names — clefts and hillocks, paths and stiles, ditches and pools; and when they found a particularly magnificent tree, they gave that a name too. In this way they took complete possession and created a little world of their own that no one else knew and no one else was at home in, and yet they had no secret which all the world might not have heard.

11.112.oldText: But love was in their hearts and was not in their hearts, as the crystals are present in a saturated solution and yet are not present — not until a splinter or the merest particle of the right matter is dropped into the solution, releasing the slumbering atoms as if by magic, and they rush to meet each other, joining and riveting themselves together according to unsearchable laws, and in the same instant there is crystal — crystal.

11.113.oldText: So it was a trifle that made them realize that they loved.

11.114.oldText: There is nothing to tell. It was a day like all other days, when they were alone together in the sitting room, as they had been a hundred times before; their conversation was about things of no moment, and what happened was outwardly as common and as everyday as possible. It was nothing more than this: Niels stood looking out of the window, and Fennimore came over to him and looked out too. That was all, but it was enough, for in a flash, like lightning, the past and present and future were transformed for Niels Lyhne by the consciousness that he loved the woman standing beside him — not as something bright and sweet and happy and beautiful that would lift him to ecstasy or rapture — such was not the nature of his love — but he loved her as something he could no more do without than the breath of life itself, and he reached out, as a drowning man clutches, and pressed her hand to his heart.

11.115.oldText: She understood him. With almost a scream, in a voice full of terror and agony, she cried out an answer and a confession: “Oh, _yes_, Niels!” and in the same instant snatched her hand away. A moment she stood, pale and shrinking, then sank down with one knee on an upholstered chair, hiding her face against the harsh velvet of the back, and sobbed aloud.

11.116.oldText: Niels stood for a few seconds as though blinded, groping among the bulb-glasses for support. It was only for a very few seconds; then he stepped over to the chair where she lay, and bent over her without touching her, resting one hand on the back of the chair.

11.117.oldText: “Don’t be so unhappy, Fennimore! Look up and let us talk about it. Will you, or won’t you? Don’t be afraid! Let us bear it together, my own love! Come, try whether you can’t!”

11.118.oldText: She raised her head slightly and looked up at him. “Oh, God, what shall we do! Isn’t it terrible, Niels! Why should such a thing happen to me? And how lovely it all might have been — so happy!” and she sobbed again.

11.119.oldText: “Should I not have spoken?” he moaned. “Poor Fennimore, would you rather never have known it?”

11.120.oldText: She raised her head again and caught his hand. “I wish I knew it and were dead. I wish I were in my grave and knew it; that would be good — oh, so peaceful and good!”

11.121.oldText: “It is bitter for us both, Fennimore, that the first thing our love brings us should be only misery and tears. Don’t you think so?”

11.122.oldText: “You must not be hard on me, Niels. I can’t help it. You can’t see it as I do — I am the one who should be strong, because I am the one who is bound. I wish I could take my love and force it back into the most secret depth of my soul and lock it in and be deaf to all its wailing and its prayers, and then tell you to go far, far away; but I can’t. I have suffered so much, I can’t suffer that as well — I can’t, Niels. I can’t live without you — there, can I? Do you think I can?”

11.123.oldText: She rose and flung herself on his breast.

11.124.oldText: “Here I am, and I won’t let you go; I won’t send you away while I sit here alone in the old darkness. It is like a bottomless pit of loathing and misery. I won’t throw myself into it. I would rather jump into the fjord, Niels. Even if the new life brings other agonies, at least they are new agonies, and don’t have the dull sting of the old ones, and can’t stab home the way the old ones do, which know my heart so cruelly well. Am I talking wildly? Yes, of course I am, but it is so good to talk to you without any reserve and without having to be careful not to say what I have no right to. For now you have the first right of all! I wish you could take me wholly, so that I belonged to you entirely and not to anyone else at all. I wish you could lift me out of all the relations that hedge me in!”

11.125.oldText: “We must break through them, Fennimore. I will arrange everything as well as possible. Don’t be afraid! Some day, before anyone suspects anything, we shall be far away.”

11.126.oldText: “No, no, we mustn’t run away, anything but that, anything else rather than have my parents hear their daughter had run away. It is impossible! I will never do it. By God in heaven, Niels, I will never do it.”

11.127.oldText: “Oh, but you must, girlie, you must. Can’t you see all the baseness and ugliness that will rise up and close in around us everywhere if we stay, all the lies and deceptions that will entangle us and drag us down? I won’t have you smeared with all of that. I refuse to let it eat into our love like corroding rust.”

11.129.oldText: “You don’t know what you are condemning us to,” he said sadly. “It would be far better to crush under iron heels now than to spare. Believe me, Fennimore, we must let our love be everything to us, the first and only thing in the world, that which must be saved, even at the cost of stabbing where we would rather heal and bringing sorrow where we would rather keep every shadow of sorrow far away. If we don’t do that, you’ll see that the yoke we bend our necks under now will weigh on us and at last force us to our knees, unmercifully, inexorably. — A fight on our knees — you don’t know how hard that is! Shall we fight the fight anyway, girlie, side by side, against everything?”

11.131.oldText: For the first few days Niels kept trying to persuade her to flee. Then he began to picture to himself what a blow it would be to Erik if he were to come home one day and find friend and wife gone away together, and by degrees the whole thing took on an unnaturally tragic air of the impossible. He schooled himself not to think of it, as he did with many other things he might have wished otherwise, and threw himself with his whole soul into the situation as it was, without any conscious attempt to make it over by dreams or to cover its defects with imaginary festoons and garlands. But, oh, how sweet it was to love, for once, with the love of real life; for now he knew that nothing of what he had imagined to be love was real love — neither the turgid longing of the lonely youth, nor the passionate yearning of the dreamer, nor yet the nervous foreboding of the child. These were currents in the ocean of love, single reflections of its full light, fragments of love the way the meteors rushing through space are splinters of a world — for that was love: a world complete in itself, fully rounded, vast, and orderly. It was no jumble of confused sensations and moods rushing one upon another! Love was like nature, ever changing, ever renewing; no feeling died and no emotion withered without giving life to the seed of something still more perfect which was embedded in it. Quietly, sanely, with full, deep breaths — it was good to love like this and love with all his soul. The days fell, bright and newly minted, down from heaven itself; they no longer followed one after another as a matter of course, like the hackneyed pictures in a peep-show. Every one of them was a revelation. With each day that passed, he felt stronger, greater, and nobler. He had never known such strength and fullness of feeling; there were moments when he seemed to himself titanic, much more than a man, so inexhaustible was the wellspring of his soul, so broad-winged the tenderness that swelled his heart, so wondrous the sweep of his vision, so infinite the gentleness of his judgments.

11.132.oldText: This was the beginning of happiness, and they were happy for a long time.

11.133.oldText: The daily falsehood and deception and the atmosphere of dishonor in which they lived had not yet gained power over them, and could not touch them on those ecstatic heights to which Niels had lifted their relationship and, with it, themselves. For he was not simply a man who seduced his friend’s wife — or rather, so he told himself defiantly, he was that man, but he was also the one who saved an innocent woman whom life had wounded, stoned, and defiled, a woman who had lain down to let her soul die. This woman he had given back her confidence in life, her faith in the powers of good; he had lifted her spirit to noble heights, had given her happiness. What, then, was better — the old blameless misery, or what he had won for her? He did not ask; he had made his choice.

11.134.oldText: He did not quite mean this, if the truth were told. Man often builds for himself theories in which he refuses to dwell. Thoughts often run faster than the sense of right and wrong is willing to follow. Yet the conception was really there in his mind, and it took some of the cankerous venom out of the craftiness, falseness, and duplicity of their lives.

11.135.oldText: Still the evil effects were soon noticeable. The poison was working on so many fine nerve-filaments that it could not fail to do harm and cause suffering, and the time was hastened when Erik, shortly after New Year, announced that he had caught hold of an idea — something with a green tunic and a threatening attitude, he told Niels. Did he remember the green in Salvator Rosa’s Jonah? Something along those lines.

11.136.oldText: Although Erik’s work consisted chiefly in lying on the couch in his studio, smoking shag and reading Marryat, it at least had the effect of keeping him at home for the time being, thereby forcing them to use more caution and to invent new lies and artifices.

11.137.oldText: Fennimore’s ingenuity in this direction was what brought the first cloud over their heaven. It was scarcely perceptible at first, only a doubt, light as thistledown, that flitted through Niels’s mind as to whether his love were not nobler than the one he loved. It had not yet taken shape as a thought; it was only a dim foreboding which pointed in that direction, a vague giving way in his mind, a leaning to that side.

11.138.oldText: Yet it came again and brought others in its wake, thoughts at first vague and indistinct, then clearer and sharper each time they appeared. It was astonishing with what furious haste these thoughts could undermine, debase, and take away the glamor. Their love was not lessened. On the contrary, it glowed more passionately while it sank; but these hand-clasps stolen under table-covers, these kisses snatched in passages and behind doors, these long looks right under the eyes of the man they deceived, took away all the lofty tenor. Happiness no longer stood still above their heads; they had to pilfer her smiles and her light as best they could, and after a while their wiles and cunning were no longer necessary evils, but amusing triumphs. Deception became their natural element and made them contemptible and petty. There were degrading secrets, too, over which they had once grieved separately, each feigning ignorance in the other’s eyes, but which they now had to share; for Erik was not bashful, and would often caress his wife in Niels’s presence, kiss her, take her on his lap, and embrace her, while Fennimore had neither courage nor dignity enough to push these caresses away; the consciousness of her guilt made her uncertain and afraid.

11.139.oldText: So it sank and went on sinking, that lofty castle of their love, from the pinnacles of which they had gazed so proudly out over the world, and within which they had felt so strong and noble.

11.140.oldText: Still they were happy among the ruins.

11.141.oldText: When they walked in the woods now, it was usually on gloomy days, when the fog hung under the dark branches and thickened between the wet trunks, so that no one would see how they kissed and embraced, both here and there, and no one would hear how their frivolous talk rang with peals of wanton laughter.

11.142.oldText: The melancholy of eternity, which had exalted their love, was gone; now there was nothing between them but smiles and jests. With feverish haste they snatched greedily at the fleeting seconds of joy, as though they had to hurry in their love and had not a lifetime before them.

11.143.oldText: It brought no change when Erik, after a while, grew tired of his idea and again began his carousing so eagerly that he was rarely at home for forty-eight hours at a stretch. Where they had fallen, there they lay. Once in a great while, perhaps, in lonely hours, they gazed regretfully toward the heights from which they had fallen, or perhaps they only wondered, and thought what a strain it must have been to stay at that level, and felt themselves more snugly housed where they now were. There was no change. At least there was no return to the former days, but the flabby uncleanness of living as they did and not running away together became more present in their consciousness and linked them together in a closer and baser union through their shared sense of guilt; for neither of them wished any change in things as they were. Nor did they pretend to each other that they did, for there had developed between them a cynical intimacy such as often exists between fellow criminals, and there was nothing in their relations that they shrank from putting into words. With sinister frankness they called things by their right names and, as they put it to themselves, faced the facts as they were.

11.145.oldText: In February it had seemed that the winter was over, but then Mother March had come shaking her white mantle with its loose lining, and snowstorm after snowstorm covered the ground with thick layers. Then followed calm weather and hard frost, and the fjord settled under a crust of ice six inches thick, which lay there a long time.

11.146.oldText: One evening toward the end of the month, Fennimore was sitting alone in her parlor after tea and waiting.

11.147.oldText: The room was brightly lit; the piano stood open with candles burning, and the silk shade had been taken off the lamp. The gilded mouldings caught the light, and the pictures on the walls seemed to stand out with a kind of vigilance. The hyacinths had been moved from the windows to the writing table, where they made a mass of delicate colors, filling the air with a penetrating fragrance that seemed cool in its purity. The fire in the stove burned with a pleasant subdued crackle.

11.148.oldText: Fennimore was walking up and down the room almost as if she were balancing on a dark red stripe in the carpet. She wore a somewhat old-fashioned black silk dress with a heavily embroidered edge that weighed it down and trailed, first on one side, then on the other, with every step she took.

11.149.oldText: She was humming to herself and holding with both hands a string of large pale yellow amber beads that hung from her neck. Whenever she wavered on the red stripe, she would stop humming, but still kept her grip on the necklace. Perhaps she was making an omen for herself: if she could walk a certain number of times up and down without stepping off the red stripe and without letting go with her hands, Niels would come.

11.150.oldText: He had been there in the morning, when Erik went away, and had stayed till late in the afternoon, but he had promised to come again as soon as the moon was up and it was light enough to see the holes in the ice on the fjord.

11.151.oldText: Fennimore had obtained her omen, whatever it was, and stepped over to the window.

11.152.oldText: It looked as if there would not be any moon tonight; the sky was very black, and the darkness must be more intense out there on the gray-blue fjord than on land, where the snow lay. Perhaps it was best that he did not attempt it. She sat down at the piano with a sigh of resignation, then got up again to look at the clock. She came back and resolutely propped up a big book of music before her, but did not play, merely turning the leaves absent-mindedly, lost in her own thoughts.

11.153.oldText: Suppose, after all, that he was standing on the opposite shore at this very moment, fastening on his skates. He could be here in an instant! She saw him plainly, a little out of breath after skating, blinking his eyes against the light on coming in from the darkness outside. He would bring a breath of cold air, and his beard would be full of tiny bright drops. Then he would say — what would he say?

11.154.oldText: She smiled and glanced down at herself.

11.155.oldText: And still the moon did not appear.

11.156.oldText: She went over to the window again and stood gazing out until the darkness seemed to fill before her eyes with tiny white sparks and rainbow-colored rings. But they were only a vague glimmer. She wished they would be transformed into fireworks out there — rockets shooting up in long, long curves and then turning to tiny snakes that bored their way into the sky and died in a flicker; or into a great, huge pale ball that hung tremulous in the sky and slowly sank down in a rain of myriad-colored stars. Look! Look! Soft and rounded like a curtsy, like a golden rain that curtsied. — Farewell! Farewell! There went the last one. — Oh dear, if he would only come! She did not want to play — and with that she turned to the piano, struck an octave harshly, and held the keys down until the tones had quite died away, then did the same again, and again, and yet again. She did not want to play, did not want to. — She would rather dance! For a moment she closed her eyes, and in imagination she felt herself whirling through a vast hall of red and white and gold. How delicious it would be to have danced and to be hot and tired and drink champagne! Suddenly she remembered how she and a school friend had concocted champagne from soda water and eau de cologne, and how sick it had made them when they drank it.

11.157.oldText: She straightened herself and walked across the room, instinctively smoothing her dress as after a dance.

11.158.oldText: “And now let us be sensible!” she said, took her embroidery and settled herself in a large armchair near the lamp.

11.159.oldText: Yet she did not work; her hands sank down into her lap, and soon she snuggled down into the chair with little lazy movements, fitting herself into its curves, her face resting on her hand, her dress wrapped around her feet.

11.160.oldText: She wondered curiously whether other wives were like her, whether they had made a mistake and been unhappy and then had loved someone else. She went over the ladies at home in Fjordby in her mind, one by one. Then she thought of Mrs. Boye. Niels had told her about Mrs. Boye, and she had always been a tantalizing riddle to her — this woman whom she hated and by whom she felt humiliated.

11.161.oldText: Erik, too, had once told her that he had been madly in love with Mrs. Boye.

11.162.oldText: Ah, if one could only know everything about her!

11.163.oldText: She laughed at the thought of Mrs. Boye’s new husband.

11.164.oldText: All the time, while her thoughts were thus engaged, she was longing and listening for Niels, and imagined him coming, always coming out there on the ice. She little guessed that for the last two hours a tiny black dot had been working its way over the snowy meadows with a message for her very different from the one she was expecting from across the fjord. It was only a man in homespun and greased boots, and now he tapped on the kitchen window, frightening the maid.

11.165.oldText: It was a letter, Trine said when she came in to her mistress. Fennimore took it. It was a telegram. Quietly she gave the maid the receipt and dismissed her; she was not in the least alarmed, for Erik of late had often telegraphed to say he would be bringing one or two guests home with him the following day.

11.167.oldText: Suddenly she turned white and darted wildly from her seat out into the middle of the room, staring at the door with expectant terror.

11.168.oldText: She would not let it come into the house, did not dare to, and with one bound she threw herself against the door, pressing her shoulder against it, and turned the key till it cut her hand. But it would not turn, no matter how hard she tried. Her hand dropped. Then she remembered that the thing was not here at all — it was far away from her in a strange house.

11.169.oldText: She began to shake; her knees would no longer support her, and she slid along the door to the floor.

11.170.oldText: Erik was dead. The horses had run away, had overturned the carriage at a street corner, and hurled Erik with his head against the wall. His skull had been fractured, and now he lay dead at Aalborg. That was the way it had happened, and most of this story was told in the telegram. No one had been with him in the carriage except the white-necked tutor known as the Arab. It was he who had telegraphed.

11.171.oldText: She crouched on the floor moaning feebly, both palms spread out on the carpet, her eyes staring with a fixed, empty look, as she swayed helplessly to and fro.

11.172.oldText: Only a moment ago everything had been light and fragrance around her, and, however much she tried, she could not instantly put all this out of her consciousness to admit the inky black night of grief and remorse. It was not her fault that her mind was still haunted by fitful, dazzling gleams of love’s happiness and love’s pleasure; that intense, foolish desires would force their way out of the whirl, seeking the bliss of forgetfulness, or trying to stop with a frenzied wrench the revolving wheel of fortune.

11.174.oldText: In black swarms, from everywhere, dark thoughts came flying like ravens, drawn by the corpse of her happiness, and hacked at it beak by beak, even while the warmth of life still lingered in it. They tore and slashed and made it hideous and unrecognizable, until the whole thing was nothing but a carrion of loathing and horror.

11.175.oldText: She rose and walked about, supporting herself by chairs and tables like someone who is ill. Desperately she looked around for some cobweb of help, if it were only a comforting glance, a sympathetic pat of the hand, but her eyes met nothing but the glaring family portraits — all the strangers who had been witnesses of her fall and her crime — sleepy old gentlemen, prim-mouthed matrons, and their ever-present gnome child, the girl with the great round eyes and bulging forehead. It had acquired memories enough at last, this strange furniture — the table over there, and that chair, the footstool with the black poodle-dog, and the portière like a dressing gown — she had saturated them all with memories, adulterous memories, which they now spewed out and flung after her. Oh, it was terrible to be locked in with all these spectres of crime and with herself. She shuddered at herself; she pointed accusing fingers at herself, at this dishonored Fennimore who crouched at her feet; she pulled her dress away from between her imploring hands. Mercy? No, there was no mercy! How could there be mercy before those dead eyes in the strange town, those eyes which had become seeing, now that they were glazed in death, and saw how she had thrown his honor in the mud, lied at his lips, been faithless at his heart.

11.176.oldText: She could feel those dead eyes riveted on her; she did not know where they came from, but they followed her, gliding down her body like two ice-cold rays. As she looked down, while every thread of the carpet, every stitch in the footstools, seemed unnaturally clear in the strong, sharp light, she felt something walking about her with the footsteps of dead men, felt it brushing against her dress so distinctly that she screamed with terror and darted to one side. But it came in front of her like hands and yet not like hands, something that clutched at her slowly, clutched derisively and triumphantly at her heart, that marvel of treachery, that yellow pearl of deceit! And she retreated till she backed up against the table, but it was still there, and her bosom gave no protection against it; it clutched through her skin and flesh.... She almost died of terror as she stood there, helplessly bending back over the table, while every nerve contracted with fear, and her eyes stared as if they were being murdered in their sockets.

11.178.oldText: She looked around with a haunted look, then sank down on her knees and prayed a long time. She repented and confessed, wildly and unrestrainedly, in growing passion, with the same fanatic self-loathing that drives the nun to scourge her naked body. She searched fervently for the most grovelling expressions, intoxicating herself with self-abasement and with a humility that thirsted for degradation.

11.179.oldText: At last she rose. Her bosom heaved violently, and there was a faint light in the pale cheeks, which seemed to have grown fuller during her prayer.

11.180.oldText: She looked around the room as if she were taking a silent vow. Then she went into the adjoining room, closed the door behind her, stood still a moment as though to accustom herself to the darkness, groped her way to the door which opened onto the glass-enclosed veranda, and went out.

11.181.oldText: It was lighter there. The moon had risen, and shone through the close-packed frozen crystals on the glass; the light came yellowish through the panes, blue and red through the squares of colored glass that framed them.

11.182.oldText: She melted a hole in the ice with her hand and carefully wiped away the moisture with her handkerchief.

11.183.oldText: As yet there was no one in sight out on the fjord.

11.184.oldText: She began to walk up and down in her glass cage. There was no furniture out there except a settee of cane and bent wood, covered with withered ivy leaves from the vines overhead. Every time she passed it, the leaves rustled faintly with the stirring of the air, and now and then her dress caught a leaf on the floor, drawing it along with a scratching sound across the boards.

11.185.oldText: Back and forth she walked on her dreary watch, her arms folded over her breast, hardening herself against the cold.

11.187.oldText: She opened the door with a quick wrench, and stepped out into the frozen snow in her thin shoes. She had no pity on herself; she could have gone barefoot to that meeting.

11.188.oldText: Niels had slowed at the sight of the black figure against the snow and was skating toward land with hesitating, tentative strokes.

11.189.oldText: That stealthy figure seemed to burn into her eyes. Every familiar movement and feature struck her as a shameless insult, as a boast of degrading secrets. She shook with hatred; her heart swelled with curses, and she could scarcely control her anger.

11.190.oldText: “It is I!” she cried out to him jeeringly, “the harlot, Fennimore!”

11.191.oldText: “But for God’s sake, sweetheart?” he asked, astonished, as he came within a few feet of her.

11.193.oldText: “Dead! When?” He had to step out onto the snow with his skates to keep from falling. “Oh, but tell me!” Eagerly he took a step nearer.

11.194.oldText: They were now standing close together, and she had to restrain herself from striking that pale, distorted face with her clenched fist.

11.195.oldText: “I will tell you, never fear,” she cried. “He is dead, as I said. He had a runaway in Aalborg and got his head crushed, while we were deceiving him here.”
