11.196.oldText: “It is terrible!” Niels moaned, pressing his hands to his temples. “Who could have dreamed — Oh, I wish we had been faithful to him, Fennimore! Erik, poor Erik! — I wish I were in his place!” He sobbed aloud, writhing with pain.

11.198.oldText: “Oh, what does it matter about us?” Niels groaned; “if we could only get him back! Poor Fennimore!” he said, with a change of feeling. “Never mind me. You hate me, you say? You may well hate me.” He rose suddenly. “Let us go in,” he said. “I don’t know what I am saying. Who was it that telegraphed, did you say?”

11.199.oldText: “In!” Fennimore screamed, infuriated by his failure to notice her hostility. “In there! Never shall you set your craven, despicable foot inside that house again. How dare you even think of it, you wretch, you false dog, who came sneaking in here and stole your friend’s honor, because it was too poorly hidden! What, did you not steal it under his very eyes, because he thought you were honest, you house-thief!”

11.200.oldText: “Hush, hush, are you mad? What is the matter with you! What sort of language are you using?” He had caught her arm firmly, drawing her toward him, and looked straight into her face in amazement. “You must try to come to your senses, child,” he said in a gentler tone. “You can’t mend matters by slinging ugly words.”

11.201.oldText: She wrenched her arm away with such force that he staggered and almost lost his uncertain foothold.

11.202.oldText: “Can’t you hear that I hate you!” she screamed shrilly. “And isn’t there so much of a decent man’s brain left in you that you can understand it! How blind I must have been when I loved you, you patched together with lies, when I had him at my side, who was ten thousand times better than you. I shall hate and despise you to the end of my life. Before you came, I was honest, I had never done anything wicked; but then you came with your poetry and your rubbish and dragged me down with your lies, into the mud with you. What have I done to you that you could not leave me alone — I, who should have been sacred to you above all others! Now I have to live day after day with this shameful blot on my soul, and I shall never meet anyone so base but that I know myself to be baser. All the memories of my girlhood you have poisoned. What have I to look back on now that is clean and good! You have tainted everything. It is not only he that is dead; everything bright and good that has been between us is dead too, and rotten. Oh, God help me, is it fair that I can’t get any revenge on you after all you have done? Make me honest again, Niels Lyhne, make me pure and good again! No, no — but it ought to be possible to torture you into undoing the wrong you have done. Can you undo it with lies? Don’t stand there and cringe under your own helplessness. I want to see you suffer, here before my eyes, and writhe in pain and despair and be miserable. Let him be miserable, God, do not let him steal my revenge too! Go, you wretch, go! I cast you off, but be sure that I drag you with me through all the agonies my hate can call down over you.”

11.203.oldText: She had stretched out her arms menacingly. Now she turned and went in, and the veranda door rattled softly as she closed it.

11.204.oldText: Niels stood looking after her in amazement, almost with disbelief. That pale, vengeful face seemed still to be there before him, so strangely base-souled and coarse, all its delicate beauty of contour gone, as if a rough, barbarous hand had ploughed up all its lines.

11.205.oldText: He stumbled cautiously down to the ice and began to skate slowly toward the mouth of the fjord, with the moonlight in front of him and the wind at his back. Gradually he increased his speed, as his thoughts took his attention from his surroundings, until the ice splinters flew from the runners of his skates and rattled on the smooth surface, blown along with him by the rising frost wind.

11.206.oldText: So that was the end! So that was the way he had saved this woman’s soul and lifted it and given it happiness! It was certainly beautiful, his relation to the dead friend, his childhood friend, for whom he would have sacrificed his future, his life, his all! He with his sacrificing and his saving! Let heaven and earth behold in him a man who preserved his life on the heights of honor without spot or blemish in order not to cast a shadow over the Idea he served and was called to promulgate.

11.207.oldText: No doubt that was another of his boastful fancies — that his paltry little life could put spots on the sun of the Idea. Good God, he was always taking these high and mighty views of himself; it was bred in his bones. If he could not be anything better, he must at least be a Judas and call himself Iscariot in grandiose gloom. That sounded like something. Was he forever going to give himself airs as if he were a responsible minister to the Idea, a member of its privy council, getting everything concerning humanity at first hand? Would he never learn to do his duty in barrack service for the Idea with all simplicity, as a private of a very subordinate class?

11.208.oldText: There were red fires out on the ice, and he skated so near them that a gigantic shadow shot out for a moment from his feet, turned forward, and disappeared again.

11.209.oldText: He thought of Erik and of what kind of friend he had been to him. He! His childhood memories wrung their hands over him; his youthful dreams covered their heads and wept over him; his whole past stared after him with a long look full of reproach. He had betrayed it all for a love as small and mean as himself. There _had_ been exaltation in this love, but he had betrayed that too.

11.210.oldText: Where could he flee to escape these attempts that always ended in the ditch? All his life had been nothing else, and it would never be anything else in the future; he knew that and felt it with such certainty that he sickened at the thought of all this futile endeavor, and he wished with all his soul that he could run away and escape this meaningless fate. If only the ice would break under him now as he skated, and all would be over with a gasp and a spasm in the cold water!

11.211.oldText: He stopped, exhausted, and looked back. The moon had gone down, and the fjord stretched long and dark between the white hills on either side. Then he turned and worked his way back against the wind. It was very strong now, and he was tired. He skated closer to the shore to get the shelter of the hills, but as he struggled along in this way, he came on a hole in the ice made by the winds sweeping down from the hills, and he felt the thin, elastic crust give way under him with a crackling sound.

11.212.oldText: Ah, he breathed more easily, in spite of everything, when he set foot on the firm ice again! Under the stimulus of fear, his exhaustion had almost left him, and he skated on vigorously.

11.214.oldText: While he was struggling out there, Fennimore sat in the lighted room, baffled and miserable. She felt herself cheated out of her revenge. She hardly knew what she had expected, but it was something entirely different; she had had a vision of something mighty and majestic, something of swords and red flames — or not that, but something that would sweep her along and lift her onto a throne, and instead it had all turned out so small and paltry, and she had felt more like a common scold than like one who utters curses....

11.215.oldText: After all, she had learned something from Niels.

11.217.oldText: Early the following morning, while Niels, overcome with exhaustion, was still asleep, she left the house.

13.0.oldText: For about a year, Niels Lyhne had lived at Lönborggaard, managing the farm as best he could, and as much as his old steward would let him. He had taken down his shield, blotted out his coat of arms, and resigned. Humanity would have to get along without him; he had come to know the joy of purely physical labor, of watching the pile grow under his hand, of being able to finish what he was doing so that he really _was_ finished, of knowing that when he walked away tired, the strength he had spent lay behind him in the work, and the work would stand there, not eaten up by doubt in the night or scattered by the breath of criticism the morning after. There were no Sisyphus stones in farming.

13.1.oldText: What a joy it was, too, after he had worked himself tired, to go to bed and gather his strength in sleep and spend it again, as regularly as day follows night, never thrown off by the caprices of his brain, never having to handle himself gingerly like a tuned guitar with loose pegs.

13.2.oldText: He was really happy, in a quiet way, and often he would sit — as his father had sat — on a stile or a boundary stone, staring out over the golden wheat or the top-heavy oats, in a strange, vegetative trance.

13.3.oldText: He had not yet begun to seek out the society of the neighboring families, except for Councillor Skinnerup’s in Varde, whom he visited quite often.

13.4.oldText: The Skinnerups had come to town while his father was still living, and since the Councillor was an old university friend of Lyhne’s, the two families had seen a lot of each other. Skinnerup, a mild, bald-headed man with sharp features and kind eyes, was now a widower, but his house was more than filled by his four daughters, the eldest seventeen, the youngest twelve.

13.5.oldText: The Councillor had read widely, and Niels enjoyed a talk with him on various aesthetic subjects — for though he had learned to use his hands, that did not, of course, turn him into a country bumpkin overnight. He was sometimes amused at the almost absurd caution he had to exercise whenever the conversation turned to a comparison between Danish and foreign literature, and in general whenever Denmark was measured against anything that wasn’t Danish. Caution was absolutely necessary, however, for the mild-mannered Councillor was one of those fierce patriots occasionally met with in those days, who might grudgingly admit that Denmark was not the greatest of the world powers, but who, with that admission made, would not grant a single jot or tittle more that might place his country, or anything belonging to it, anywhere but at the head of the list.

13.6.oldText: These conversations had another charm, which Niels felt at first only vaguely and without consciously noticing it: the look of delighted admiration with which seventeen-year-old Gerda’s eyes followed him as he spoke. She always managed to be present when he came, and would listen so eagerly that he often saw her flush with rapture when he said something that struck her as especially beautiful.

13.7.oldText: The truth was that, without meaning to, he had become this young lady’s ideal — at first chiefly because he often rode into town wearing a gray mantle of a very foreign and romantic cut; then because he always said Milano instead of Milan; and finally because he was alone in the world and had a rather sad face. There were certainly a great many ways in which he differed from the rest of the people in Varde, and in Ringkjøbing too.

13.9.oldText: On a hot summer day Niels came walking through the narrow street behind the Councillor’s garden. The sun was pouring down on the brick-red little houses, and the ships lying out on the sound had mats hung over their sides to keep the tar from melting and oozing out of the seams. Everything around him was thrown open to let in a coolness that wasn’t there. Inside the open doors, children were reading their lessons aloud, and the hum of their voices mingled with the hum of the bees in the garden, while a flock of sparrows hopped silently from tree to tree, all flying up together and coming down together.

13.10.oldText: Niels stepped into a little house right behind the garden, and while the woman went to fetch her husband from the neighbor’s, he was left alone in a spotless little room that smelled of gillyflowers and freshly ironed linen.

13.11.oldText: When he had examined the pictures on the walls, the two china dogs on the dresser, and the seashells on the lid of the work-box, he stepped over to the open window, from which he could hear Gerda’s voice — and there were the four Skinnerup girls on the Councillor’s bleaching-green, only a few steps away.

13.12.oldText: The balsamines and other flowers in the window hid him, and he made ready both to listen and to look.

13.13.oldText: It was clear that a quarrel was going on, and the three younger sisters were making common cause against Gerda. All of them carried whips of lemon-yellow willow withes. The youngest had twisted three or four of hers into rings wound about with red bark, and had set them on her head like a turban.

13.14.oldText: It was she who was speaking.

13.15.oldText: “She says he looks like Themistocles on the stove in the study,” she remarked to her fellow conspirators, and turned up her eyes with a rapt expression.

13.16.oldText: “Oh, pshaw,” said the middle one, a saucy little lady who had just been confirmed that spring; “do you suppose Themistocles was round-shouldered?” She imitated Niels Lyhne’s slight stoop. “Themistocles! Not likely!”

13.17.oldText: “There is something so manly in his look; he is a real man!” quoted the twelve-year-old.

13.18.oldText: “He!” came the middle one’s voice again. “Why, he goes around pouring eau de cologne on himself. The other day his gloves were lying there and simply reeking with millefleurs.”

13.19.oldText: “_Every_ perfection!” breathed the twelve-year-old in ecstasy, and staggered back as if overcome.

13.20.oldText: They addressed all this to one another and pretended not to notice Gerda, who was standing a little apart, blushing furiously as she poked at the ground with her yellow stick. Suddenly she lifted her head.

13.21.oldText: “You’re a pair of naughty hussies,” she said, “to talk like that about someone who is too good even to look at you.”

13.22.oldText: “And yet you know he is _only_ a mortal,” the eldest of the three remonstrated mildly, as if to make peace.

13.24.oldText: “And _surely_ he has his faults,” her sister went on, pretending not to hear what Gerda said.

13.26.oldText: “But, my dear Gerda, you _know_ he never goes to church.”

13.27.oldText: “What should he go there for? He knows _ever_ so much more than the pastor.”

13.28.oldText: “Yes, but unfortunately he doesn’t believe in any God _at all_, Gerda.”

13.29.oldText: “Well, you can be very sure, my dear, that if he doesn’t, he has _excellent_ reasons for it.”

13.30.oldText: “Why, Gerda, how can you say such a thing!”

13.31.oldText: “You’d almost think —” the middle one broke in.

13.32.oldText: “What would you almost think?” Gerda snapped.

13.33.oldText: “Nothing, nothing at all. Please don’t bite me!” the sister replied, with a sudden air of great meekness.

13.34.oldText: “You’ll tell me this instant what you meant!”

13.35.oldText: “No, no, no, no, no; I guess I have a right to hold my tongue if I want to.”

13.36.oldText: She walked off together with the twelve-year-old, each with her arm around the other’s shoulder in sisterly accord. The eldest followed them, strutting with indignation.

13.37.oldText: Gerda, left alone, stood looking straight ahead defiantly, cutting at the air with her yellow stick.

13.38.oldText: There was a moment of silence, and then the thin voice of the twelve-year-old came floating up from the other end of the garden, singing:

13.39.oldText: “_You ask me, my lad, What I want with the withered flower_ —”

13.40.oldText: Niels understood the teasing perfectly, for he had recently given Gerda a book with a dried vine leaf from the garden in Verona that contains Juliet’s grave. He could hardly keep from laughing; but just then the woman returned with her husband, whom she had finally found, and Niels had to give the order for the carpentry work he had come about.

13.41.oldText: From that day on Niels watched Gerda more closely, and every time he saw her he felt more keenly how sweet and fine she was. As time went on, his thoughts turned more and more often to this trusting little girl.

13.42.oldText: She was very lovely, with the tender, appealing kind of beauty that almost brings tears to the eyes. Her figure, in its early ripening, still kept something of the child’s roundness, which lent an air of innocence to her lush womanhood. The small, softly molded hands were losing the pink of adolescence, and they showed none of the restless, nervous curiosity so often seen at that age. She had a strong little neck, cheeks rounded in a large, full line, and a low, dreamy little woman’s forehead, where great thoughts were strangers and seemed almost to hurt when they came, bringing a frown to the thick brows. And her eye — how deep and blue it lay there, but deep only as a lake in which one can see the bottom; and in its soft corners the smile brooded happily under lids that lifted in slow surprise. This was how she looked, little Gerda — white and pink and blonde, all her short, bright hair demurely gathered into a knot.

13.43.oldText: Niels and Gerda had many a talk, and he fell more and more in love with her. Open and frank and chivalrous his regard remained — until a certain day when there came a change in the air between them, a gleam of that which is too imponderable to be called sensuousness and yet belongs to the senses, that which moves hand and mouth and eyes to reach out for what the heart cannot get close enough to its own heart. And another day, not long after, Niels went to Gerda’s father, because Gerda was so young, and because he was so sure of her love. And her father said yes, and Gerda said yes.

13.44.oldText: In the spring they were married.

13.46.oldText: It seemed to Niels Lyhne that existence had grown wonderfully clear and uncomplicated, that life was simple to live and happiness as near and as easy to win as the air he drew in with his breath.

13.47.oldText: He loved her, the young wife he had won, with all the delicacy of thought and feeling, with all the large, deep tenderness of a man who knows how love tends to sink and who believes in the power of love to rise. How he guarded this young soul that bent toward him with infinite trust and pressed up against him in caressing faith, in implicit confidence that he would do her nothing but good, as the ewe lamb in the parable must have felt toward its shepherd when it ate from his hand and drank from his cup! He had not the heart to take her God away from her or to banish all those white hosts of angels that fly singing through the heavens all day and come to earth at evening and spread their wings from bed to bed, watching faithfully and filling the darkness of night with a protecting wall of invisible light. He shrank from letting his own heavier, imageless view of life come between her and the soft blue of the heavens and make her feel uneasy and forsaken.

13.48.oldText: But she would have it otherwise. She wanted to share everything with him; there must be no place in heaven or on earth where their ways parted. Whatever he said to hold her back, she met it all, if not with the words of the Moabite woman, then with the same stubborn thought that lay in those words — thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.

13.49.oldText: So he began to teach her in earnest. He explained to her that all gods were the work of human beings and, like everything else human beings make, could not last forever, but had to pass away, generation after generation of gods — because humanity is constantly developing and outgrowing its own ideals. A god on whom the noblest and greatest of men could not lavish the richest gifts of their spirit, a god that did not draw its light from human beings but had to give light by virtue of its own being, a god that did not develop but stiffened in the historical plaster of dogmas — such a god was no longer a god, but an idol. And therefore Judaism had been right against Baal and Astarte, and Christianity had been right against Judaism, for an idol is nothing in the world. Humanity had gone on from god to god, and therefore Christ could say, on the one hand, looking back to the old God, that He had not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it, while on the other hand He could point beyond Himself to a yet higher ideal in those mystical words about the sin that shall not be forgiven, the sin against the Holy Ghost.

13.50.oldText: He went on to teach her that faith in a personal God who guides everything for the best and punishes and rewards beyond the grave is a running away from the harsh realities of life, a helpless attempt to take the sting out of its arbitrariness. He showed her that it must blunt compassion and make people less ready to strain every nerve to relieve suffering, since they could soothe themselves with the thought that pain in this brief earthly life paved the way for the sufferer to an eternity of glory and joy.

13.51.oldText: He emphasized the strength and self-reliance humanity would gain once people had learned to have faith in themselves, and once the individual set himself to bring his life into harmony with what seemed to him, in his best moments, the highest that dwelt within him, instead of seeking it outside himself in a ruling deity. He made his faith as beautiful and blessed as he could, but he did not hide from her how crushingly sad and comfortless the truth of atheism would look in the hour of sorrow compared with the old, fair, happy dream of a Heavenly Father who guides and rules. And yet she was brave. It is true that many of his doctrines — often the very ones he had least expected to affect her — would shake her to the innermost depths of her soul, but her faith knew no bounds; her love carried her with him away from all heavens, and she believed because she loved. Then, after a while, when the new ideas had grown familiar and homelike, she became intolerant in the highest degree and fanatical, as young disciples always are who love their master intensely. Niels often reproached her for it, but that was the one thing she could never understand — that when their own belief was the true one, the belief of others should not be horrible and reprehensible.

13.52.oldText: For three years they lived happily together, and much of that happiness shone from a baby face, the face of a little boy who had been born to them in the second year of their marriage.

13.53.oldText: Happiness usually makes people good, and Niels worked earnestly to make their lives so beautiful, noble, and useful that there should never be any pause in the growth of their souls toward the human ideal in which they both believed. But he no longer thought of carrying the standard of his ideal out into the world; he was content to follow it. Once in a while he would take out some of his old attempts, and then he always wondered whether it was really he who had written these pretty, artistic things. His own verses invariably brought tears to his eyes, but he would not for anything in the world have changed places with the poor fellow who wrote them.

13.54.oldText: Suddenly, in the spring, Gerda fell ill and could not recover.

13.55.oldText: Early one morning — it was the last — Niels was sitting up with her. The sun was about to rise and cast a red glow on the white shade curtains, though the light coming in on either side was still blue, making blue shadows in the folds of the white bed-spread and under Gerda’s pale, thin hands, which lay clasped before her on the sheet. Her cap had slipped off, and, as her head lay far back on the pillow, her features, sharpened and refined by suffering, had an unfamiliar and strangely distinguished air. She moved her lips as if to moisten them, and Niels reached for a glass holding a dark red liquid, but she shook her head faintly. Then suddenly she turned her face to him and gazed anxiously into his mournful countenance. As she looked at the deep sorrow his face revealed, and the despair it could not hide, her uneasy foreboding changed gradually into a terrible certainty.

13.56.oldText: She struggled to sit up, but could not.

13.57.oldText: Niels bent over her quickly, and she caught his hand.

13.58.oldText: “Is it death?” she asked, lowering her weak voice as if she could not bear to speak the words.

13.59.oldText: He could only look at her, while his breath came in a deep, moaning sigh.

13.60.oldText: Gerda clutched his hand and threw herself over to him in her fear. “I don’t dare,” she said.

13.61.oldText: He sank to his knees by the bed and put his arm under the pillow so that he almost held her to his breast. He could hardly see her for the tears that blinded him as they ran down his cheeks one after another, and he lifted her hand with a corner of the sheet to his eyes. Then he mastered his voice. “Tell me everything, Gerda dear; never mind me. Is it the pastor?” He could hardly believe it was that, and there was a note of doubt in his voice.

13.62.oldText: She did not answer, but closed her eyes and drew her head back a little, as if to be alone with her thoughts.

13.63.oldText: A few minutes passed. The soft, long-drawn whistle of a blackbird sounded underneath the windows; then another whistled, and another; a whole run of flute-like notes pierced the silence of the room.

13.64.oldText: Then she looked up again. “If you were with me,” she said, and she leaned more heavily on the pillow he was supporting. There was a caress in the movement, and he felt it. “If you were with me! But alone!”

13.65.oldText: She drew his hand toward her feebly and let it drop again. “I don’t dare.” Her eyes were full of fear. “You must fetch him, Niels, I don’t dare go up there alone like this. We had never thought that I would die first; it was always going to be you who went before. Yes, I know — but suppose, after all, we have been wrong; we _might_ have been wrong, Niels, mightn’t we? You don’t think so, but it would be strange if _everybody_ should be mistaken, and if there were nothing at all — those big churches and the bells when they bury people — I have always been so fond of the bells.” She lay quite still, as if listening for them and able to hear them.

13.66.oldText: “It is impossible, Niels, that it should all be over when we die. You don’t feel it, you who are well, you think it must quite kill us, because we are so weak, and everything seems to slip away; but it is only the world outside, inside us there is just as much soul as before. It is there, Niels; I have it all within me, everything that has been given me, the same infinite world, but quieter, more alone with itself, the way it is when you close your eyes. It is just like a candle, Niels, being carried away from you into the darkness, into the darkness, and it seems fainter and fainter to you, and you can’t see it any more, but still it is shining over there where it is — far away. I always thought I would live to be such an old, old woman, and that I would stay here with you all, and now they won’t let me, they are taking me away from house and home and making me go all alone. I am afraid, Niels, that where I am going it is God who rules, and He cares nothing for our cleverness here on earth. He wants His own way and nothing else, but somehow everything of His is so far from me. I haven’t done anything very wicked, have I? But it isn’t that.... Go and get the pastor, I want him so much.”

13.67.oldText: Niels rose and went for the pastor at once; he was grateful that this had not come at the very last moment.

13.68.oldText: The pastor came and was left alone with Gerda.

13.69.oldText: He was a handsome, middle-aged man with finely cut, regular features and large brown eyes. He knew, of course, Niels Lyhne’s attitude to the church, and now and then some expressions of hostility that had sprung from the young wife’s fanaticism had been reported to him; but he never for a moment thought of speaking to her as to a heathen or an apostate, for he understood perfectly that it was only her love that had led her astray, and he also understood the feeling that moved her now, when love could no longer follow her, to seek reconciliation with the God she had once known. And so, in his talk with her, he tried to wake her dormant memories by reading to her the passages from the Gospels and the hymns he thought would be most familiar to her.

13.71.oldText: The words woke intimate and solemn echoes in her soul, like the ringing of bells on Christmas morning. Instantly there was spread before her eyes the land where our imagination is first at home, where Joseph dreamed and David sang, and where the ladder stands that reaches from earth to heaven. It lay there with figs and mulberries, and the Jordan gleamed like clearest silver in the morning mist; Jerusalem stood red and somber under the setting sun; but over Bethlehem there was always a glorious night with great stars in the deep blue vault. How her childhood faith welled up again! She was once more the little girl who went to church clinging to her mother’s hand and sat there shivering with cold and wondering why people sinned so much. Then she grew again to full stature beneath the lofty words of the Sermon on the Mount, and she lay there like a sinner prostrate while the pastor spoke of the sacred mysteries of baptism and of Holy Communion. At last the true longing rose in her heart: the meek kneeling before the almighty and judging God, the bitter tears of remorse before the betrayed and reviled and tortured God, and the humbly audacious desire for the new covenant of wine and bread with the hidden God.

13.72.oldText: The pastor left her. Toward noon he came back and gave her the sacrament.

13.73.oldText: Her strength waned in a fitful flicker; yet at dusk, when Niels took her in his arms for the last time to say farewell before the shadows of death came too near, she was fully conscious. But the love that had been the purest joy of his life had gone out of her eyes; she was no longer his; even now her wings were growing, and she yearned only for her God.

13.75.oldText: The months that followed were dreary. Time seemed to swell up into something huge and hostile; every day was an unending desert of emptiness, every night a hell of memories. The summer was almost over before the rushing, foaming torrent of his grief had hollowed out a river-bed in his soul where it could flow in a heavy, murmuring stream of sadness and longing.

13.76.oldText: Then one day, coming home from the fields, he found his little boy very ill. The child had been ailing for several days and had been restless in the night, but no one had taken it for anything serious; now he lay in his little bed hot and cold with fever and moaning with pain.

13.77.oldText: The carriage was sent at once to Varde for a physician, but none of the doctors was at home, and it had to wait for hours. At bedtime it had still not returned.

13.78.oldText: Niels sat by the child’s cot. Every half hour, or oftener, he would send someone out to listen and look for the carriage. A mounted messenger was also sent to meet it, but he failed to see any carriage and rode all the way to Varde.

13.79.oldText: This waiting for help that did not come made it all the more agonizing to watch the suffering of the sick child. The illness moved fast. Toward eleven the first attack of convulsions set in, and after that they came again and again at shorter and shorter intervals.

13.80.oldText: A little after one, the mounted messenger returned, saying that the carriage could not be expected for some hours yet, since none of the doctors had been at home when he rode out of town.

13.81.oldText: Then Niels broke down. He had fought against his despair as long as there was any hope, but now he could fight no more. He went into the dark parlor next to the sickroom and stared out through the dusky panes, while his nails dug into the wood of the casement. His eyes seemed to burrow into the darkness for some hope; his brain crouched for a spring up toward a miracle; then suddenly everything was still and clear for an instant, and in the clearness he turned away from the window to a table standing there, threw himself across it, and sobbed without tears.

13.82.oldText: When he came back into the sickroom, the child was in convulsions. He looked at him as if he meant to stab himself to death with the sight: the tiny hands clenched and white, with bluish nails, the staring eyes rolling in their sockets, the mouth distorted, the teeth grinding with a sound like iron on stone — it was terrible, and yet that was not the worst. No, worst was this: when the convulsions stopped and the body grew soft again, relaxing with the happy relief of lessened pain, and then to see the terror come into the child’s eyes when he felt the first faint approach of the convulsions returning, the growing plea for help as the pain came closer and closer — to see this and not be able to help, not with his heart’s blood, not with all he possessed! He lifted his clenched hands threateningly to heaven, he caught up his child in a mad impulse of flight, and then he threw himself down on the floor on his knees, praying to the Lord Who is in heaven, Who keeps the earth in fear through trials and chastisements, Who sends want and sickness, suffering and death, Who demands that every knee shall bend to Him in trembling, from Whom no flight is possible — either at the uttermost ends of the ocean or in the depths of the earth — He, the God Who, if it pleases Him, will tread the one you love best under His foot, torture him back into the dust from which He Himself created him.

13.83.oldText: With such thoughts Niels Lyhne sent prayers up to God; he threw himself down in utter abandonment before the heavenly throne, confessing that power was His and His alone.

13.85.oldText: Toward morning, when the old family doctor drove in through the gate, Niels was alone.

14.0.oldText: Autumn had come; there were no flowers any more on the graves in the churchyard, and the fallen leaves lay brown and moldering in the wet under the trees at Lönborggaard.

14.1.oldText: Niels Lyhne moved through the empty rooms in bitter despondency. Something had given way in him the night the child died. He had lost faith in himself, lost his belief in human beings’ power to bear the life they had to live. Existence had sprung a leak, and its contents were seeping out through every crack without plan or purpose.

14.2.oldText: It was no use telling himself that the prayer he had prayed was only a father’s frenzied cry for help for his child — a cry uttered even though he knew no one could hear it. He had known perfectly well what he was doing, even in the depths of his despair. He had been tempted, and he had fallen; for a fall it was, a betrayal of himself and his ideal. No doubt tradition had run too strong in his blood. Humanity had cried out to heaven in its agony for many thousands of years, and he had given in to an inherited instinct. But he ought to have resisted, for he knew with the innermost fibers of his brain that gods were dreams, and he knew that when he prayed he was taking refuge in a dream, just as surely as he had known, in the old days when he threw himself into the arms of his fancies, that they _were_ fancies. He had not been able to bear life as it was. He had taken his place in the battle for the highest, and in the heat of the fight he had deserted the banner he had sworn to defend; for after all, the new ideal, atheism, the sacred cause of truth — what was any of it but a grand name for one simple thing: to bear life as it was! To bear life as it was and let it shape itself according to its own laws!

14.3.oldText: It seemed to him as though his life had ended in that night of agony. What came after was no more than meaningless scenes tacked on after the fifth act, when the action was already finished. He could, of course, take up his old principles again if he felt so inclined, but he had once fallen, and whether or not he fell again made absolutely no difference.

14.4.oldText: This was the mood that held him most often.

14.5.oldText: Then came the November day when the King died, and war seemed more and more imminent.

14.6.oldText: He soon settled his affairs at Lönborggaard and enlisted as a volunteer.

14.7.oldText: The monotony of training was easy to bear, for it felt wonderful simply to know that he was no longer superfluous; and when he was sent into active service, the constant fight against cold, vermin, and every kind of discomfort drove his thoughts home and kept them from wandering farther than what lay right at his door. He grew almost cheerful over it, and his health, which had suffered under the griefs of the past year, was fully restored.

14.8.oldText: On a gloomy day in March he was shot in the chest.

14.9.oldText: Hjerrild, who was a physician at the hospital, had him placed in a small room with only four beds. One of the men there had been shot in the spine and lay quite still. Another was wounded in the chest and lay for hours at a time talking deliriously in quick, abrupt phrases. The third, who lay nearest to Niels, was a great strong peasant lad with fat, round cheeks; he had been struck in the brain by a fragment of a shell, and without stopping, hour after hour, about every half minute, he would lift his right arm and his right leg at the same time and then let them fall again, accompanying the movement with a loud but dull, hollow “Hah-ho!” — always in the same beat, always exactly the same — “Hah” as he raised his limbs, “ho” as he let them drop.

14.10.oldText: There Niels Lyhne lay. The bullet had entered his right lung and had not come out again. In wartime there is little room for tact, and he was told that he had little chance of survival.

14.11.oldText: He was surprised; he did not feel as though he were dying, and his wound did not hurt him much. But soon a faintness came over him and warned him that the doctor was right.

14.12.oldText: So this was the end. He thought of Gerda; he thought of her constantly the first day, but he was always disturbed by the strange, cool look in her eyes the last time he had taken her in his arms. How beautiful it would have been, how piercingly beautiful, if she had clung to him to the very last and had sought his eye until her own was glazed in death; if she had been content to breathe out her life upon the heart that loved her so well, instead of turning away from him at the last moment to save herself over into more life and still more life!

14.13.oldText: On his second day in the hospital, Niels felt more and more oppressed by the heavy air in the room, and his longing for fresh air became strangely entangled in his mind with the desire to live. After all, there had been so much in life that was beautiful, he thought, as he remembered the fresh breeze along the shore at home, the cool rustling of the wind in the beech forests of Sjælland, the pure mountain air of Clarens, and the evening breezes of Lake Garda. But as soon as he began to think of other people, his soul sickened again. He called them up in review before him, one by one, and they all passed and left him alone, and not one stayed. But how far had he held on to them himself? Had he been true? He had only been slower in letting go — that was all. No, it was _not_ even that. It was the bleak truth that a soul is always alone. Every belief in the fusing of soul with soul was a lie. Not your mother who took you on her lap, nor your friend, nor even the wife who slept on your heart....

14.14.oldText: Toward evening, inflammation set in and the pain of the wound grew worse.

14.15.oldText: Hjerrild came and sat with him for a few minutes in the evening, and at midnight he came back and stayed a long while. Niels was suffering intensely and moaning with pain.

14.16.oldText: “A word in all seriousness, Lyhne,” said Hjerrild. “Do you want to see a clergyman?”

14.17.oldText: “I have no more to do with clergymen than you have,” Niels whispered angrily.

14.18.oldText: “Never mind about me! I am alive and well. Don’t lie there and torture yourself with your opinions. People who are about to die have no opinions, and the ones they do have don’t matter. Opinions are only for the living — in life they can do some good, but what difference does it make whether you die with one opinion or another? Listen, we all have bright, tender memories from our childhood; I have seen scores of people die, and it always comforts them to bring those memories back. Let us be honest! Whatever we call ourselves, we can never quite get that God out of heaven; our brain has pictured Him up there too often, the image has been rung into it and sung into it from the time we were little children.”

14.20.oldText: Hjerrild bent down to catch his words if he wanted to say anything.

14.21.oldText: “You are very good,” Niels whispered, “but” — and he shook his head decisively.

14.22.oldText: The room was quiet for a long time, except for the peasant lad’s everlasting “Hah-ho!” hammering the hours to pieces.

14.23.oldText: Hjerrild rose. “Good-bye, Lyhne,” he said. “After all, it is a noble death to die for our poor country.”

14.24.oldText: “Yes,” said Niels, “and yet this isn’t the way we dreamed of doing our part, long, long ago.”

14.25.oldText: Hjerrild left him. When he came into his own room he stood for a long while by the window, looking up at the stars.

14.26.oldText: “If I were God,” he said under his breath, and in his thoughts he went on, “I would much rather save the man who was _not_ converted at the last moment.”

14.27.oldText: The pain in Niels’s wound grew more and more intense; it tore and clutched at his chest, it would not let up. What a relief it would have been if he had had a god to whom he could moan and pray!

14.28.oldText: Toward morning he grew delirious; the inflammation was spreading rapidly.

14.29.oldText: So it went on for two more days and two more nights.

14.30.oldText: The last time Hjerrild saw Niels Lyhne, he was babbling of his armor and of how he must die standing.

14.31.oldText: And at last he died the death — the difficult death.
